Article Title: Over 1 million evacuated as Typhoon Dolphin hits eastern China; 1,400 Shanghai flights cancelled
Article Text:
China issues red alert as Typhoon Dolphin approaches. (Photo: ANI)

More than a million people were evacuated across eastern China, including Shanghai, after Typhoon Dolphin made landfall on Sunday, bringing transport services across the region to a halt and raising fears of flooding and landslides.Dolphin first struck Yuhuan in Zhejiang province at 5.30pm local time, with maximum wind speeds of 150kmph, meteorological authorities said. It made a second landfall in the city of Wenzhou about an hour later.The storm caused widespread travel disruption, with 1,400 flights cancelled in Shanghai alone.Chinese authorities had earlier issued their highest-level red alert for Dolphin. According to the BBC, the typhoon had been downgraded to a tropical storm by Monday morning.Despite the downgrade, the system continued to move inland, with authorities warning of torrential rain, severe flooding and landslides through Wednesday.Heavy rain was forecast on Monday across Shandong, Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu and Zhejiang provinces, as well as Shanghai.Local governments urged people to avoid outdoor activities as a precaution. Several major tourist attractions remained closed, including parts of Disneyland and Legoland, along with a number of viewing platforms on Shanghai's Bund waterfront.
Article Summary: Dolphin first struck Yuhuan in Zhejiang province at 5.30pm local time, with maximum wind speeds of 150kmph. It made a second landfall in the city of Wenzhou about an hour later. 1,400 flights cancelled in Shanghai alone.

Article Title: More than 20 US warships deployed against Iran in Hormuz; 55 vessels redirected
Article Text:
More than 20 US warships are currently deployed to the Middle East for military missions, including the naval blockade against Iran, according to CENTCOM.

US Central Command (Centcom) said on Monday that its forces had redirected 55 commercial vessels, disabled two and boarded two others while enforcing Washington’s naval blockade against Iran. More than 20 US warships remain deployed across the Middle East to sustain the operation.In a post on X, Centcom said, "US Sailors stand watch on the bridge of USS Ross (DDG 71). Ross is one of over 20 U.S. warships deployed to the Middle East supporting military missions, including strict enforcement of the US blockade against Iran.""As of Aug. 9, CENTCOM has redirected 55 commercial vessels, disabled 2, and boarded 2 to ensure compliance," it added.The latest figures marked an increase from an earlier update in which Centcom said 53 commercial vessels had been redirected, while two had been disabled and two boarded. The US military has also allowed vessels carrying humanitarian aid to pass through the blockade.Earlier, The Wall Street Journal reported that US president Donald Trump appeared to be seeking an exit from the military confrontation with Iran as the conflict grows increasingly difficult to resolve.The report said the administration may be willing to set aside the nuclear issue and declare victory if Tehran fully reopens the Strait of Hormuz.In another post, Centcom said, "US Sailors conduct maintenance on F/A-18E Super Hornets on the flight deck of aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN 72) to ensure carrier strike group assets remain mission ready to enforce the U.S. blockade against Iran. As of Aug. 8, CENTCOM redirected 53 commercial vessels, disabled 2, and boarded 2. The U.S. military has also permitted more than 30 ships to pass through the blockade for humanitarian aid. "The maritime measures come amid heightened tensions around the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil shipments, as Washington continues to pressure Tehran.Meanwhile, Trump signalled on Sunday that the administration was favouring economic pressure over a fresh military offensive against Iran, Axios reported."We are low keying it," Axios quoted Trump as saying.Trump said the US was only "semi-negotiating" with Iran while monitoring its economic situation."We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money," Trump added, according to Axios.The comments came as the US military continued its maritime enforcement operation. A US-Iran-Oman agreement that would give Tehran partial control over the Strait of Hormuz traffic remains pending. Earlier, US vice president JD Vance said Washington was working to establish a route that would allow commercial vessels to safely transit the Strait of Hormuz while maintaining pressure on Iran.
Article Summary: US Central Command (Centcom) said on Monday that its forces had redirected 55 commercial vessels, disabled two and boarded two others while enforcing Washington’s naval blockade against Iran. More than 20 US warships remain deployed across the Middle East to sustain the operation.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Arthur Schopenhauer: 'Talent hits a target no one else can hit. Genius hits a target no one else can see' and the philosophy behind revolutionary thinking
Article Text:
Arthur Schopenhauer

“Talent hits a target no one else can hit. Genius hits a target no one else can see,”

A lonely philosopher’s view of human ability

The World as Will and Representation

Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung

The philosophy of seeing beyond the self

Knowing the difference between optimization and real innovation

For known problems, use talent. Improve your techniques, learn established methods and practice carefully until you can meet clear goals more effectively.

Improve your techniques, learn established methods and practice carefully until you can meet clear goals more effectively. For problems caused by stagnation, make room for genius. Question basic assumptions, step away from immediate measurements and ask what possibilities are being ignored simply because they do not fit current systems.

An archer steps up to the line, pulls back the bowstring and releases an arrow that hits a bullseye two hundred yards away through thick fog. The crowd applauds the incredible skill needed to make a shot that almost nobody else could manage.Then another marksman steps forward, turns forty-five degrees away from the target range and fires an arrow into an empty part of the forest. Moments later, a target that nobody knew was hanging there falls from a high branch.wrote the German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer.The difference challenges the common idea that talent and genius are simply different levels of the same ability. Talent is a quantitative advantage. It means being extremely good at working within existing rules, tools and systems. Genius is different. It is a qualitative change: the ability to see possibilities that other people do not even recognize.Arthur Schopenhauer published this metaphor in the expanded 1844 edition of), in Chapter 31, titled “On Genius.”In the original German, Schopenhauer wrote: “Das Talent gleicht dem Schützen, der ein Ziel trifft, welches die Uebrigen nicht erreichen können; das Genie dem, der eines trifft, bis zu welchem sie nicht ein Mal zu sehn vermögen.”When Schopenhauer wrote these words in 1844, he was a bitter and largely ignored academic living in Frankfurt. The first edition of his major work, published in late 1818, had been a commercial failure. Many copies were eventually sold as wastepaper. For years, he watched contemporaries such as Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel receive fame, university positions and public admiration, while Schopenhauer’s own university lectures attracted very few students.Schopenhauer believed that talent usually belongs to its own time. A talented person becomes highly skilled at answering questions that society is already asking. Because their abilities fit existing needs, they can receive recognition, money and praise quickly.Genius works differently. Schopenhauer compared it to something like a comet entering an orderly planetary system. Because a genius works toward a goal that other people cannot yet understand, their ideas may be met with silence, confusion or even hostility during their lifetime.To understand this difference, we need to look at Schopenhauer’s larger theory of consciousness. He argued that ordinary human thinking is controlled by what he called the “Will”—a blind and constant drive toward survival, self-interest and reproduction.Talent usually works in service of this Will. A talented person uses a powerful intellect to solve practical problems, win competitions or master an existing craft. Their mind may be extremely sharp, but it remains connected to personal goals and the demands of society.Genius appears when the intellect can temporarily escape these demands. Schopenhauer described genius as the ability to enter a state of “pure contemplation.” In this state, a person becomes deeply objective and temporarily forgets their ego, desires and personal situation in order to see things more clearly.Because the genius is less controlled by immediate practical needs, they can notice fundamental truths, artistic forms or scientific principles that other people overlook.This helps explain why major discoveries can sometimes look strange or even foolish to people living at the time. When Gregor Mendel discovered the basic laws of genetic inheritance through his pea plant experiments in 1866, the scientific world largely ignored his published work. It took about thirty-five years for his findings to receive serious recognition. Mendel had identified important patterns of heredity at a time when biology did not yet have the concepts or language needed to fully understand what he had found.In 2026, Schopenhauer’s distinction remains useful for thinking about business, technology and personal development.Modern culture often mistakes extreme optimization for genius. High-frequency trading systems, machine-learning models that break performance records and highly efficient supply chains can represent extraordinary levels of talent. They hit known targets with speeds and accuracy that ordinary people cannot match.But true genius can change the target itself.Consider the development of personal computing and digital media. While many traditional companies were focused on improving existing systems, researchers such as Alan Kay at Xerox PARC were imagining graphical user interfaces, object-oriented programming and portable computers. These ideas went beyond simply making existing tools faster or more efficient. They suggested entirely different ways of interacting with technology.Schopenhauer’s idea can therefore help us decide what kind of thinking a problem requires.Talent is the ability to hit a target that others struggle to reach. Genius is the ability to notice that there is another target altogether.Schopenhauer understood that talent often receives quick recognition because it solves the problems of its own time. Genius is different. It may produce ideas that seem useless, strange or impossible at first because society does not yet know what to do with them.The genius therefore works ahead of the crowd, aiming at something that others cannot yet see. Recognition may come much later, when the world finally catches up with the target.
Article Summary: Arthur Schopenhauer: Talent is a quantitative advantage. Genius is a qualitative change: the ability to see possibilities that other people do not even recognize. A talented person becomes highly skilled at answering questions that society is already asking. Genius appears when the intellect can temporarily escape these demands.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Zhuangzi: 'Rewards and punishment is the lowest form of education' and why carrots and sticks can kill the desire to learn
Article Text:
Zhuangzi was an ancient Chinese philosopher who championed freedom, natural living, and inner wisdom over forced rules and external rewards.

“Rewards and punishment is the lowest form of education,”

The philosopher who chose a mud puddle over a throne

The trap of external motivation

Why this ancient idea still matters

When a carrot or a stick is needed to make a person act, the inner desire to do the task has already been lost.wrote the ancient Chinese philosopher Zhuangzi.This idea challenges the way institutions teach and control people. Modern education systems often depend on external controls: grades, test rankings, detention, honor rolls and the fear of failure. Zhuangzi’s statement suggests that depending on these tools is not real education, but a form of conditioning. It treats students like animals that must be driven, instead of seeing them as independent minds. External rewards and punishments replace genuine understanding with a simple transaction: do this and you get something; refuse, and you are punished.Master Zhuang, known as Zhuangzi or Chuang Tzu, lived during the Warring States period of ancient China, around the fourth century BCE. This was a time of political chaos, changing borders and intense competition between thinkers who were trying to find ways to bring order to a divided society.Unlike Confucius, who emphasized social roles, ceremonies, duties and organized moral government, Zhuangzi became one of the central figures of Daoism.He believed that too many artificial rules and government controls could damage human nature instead of improving it.The historical record Shiji, written by Han dynasty historian Sima Qian, tells a famous story about Zhuangzi. The King of Chu sent messengers to offer him the respected position of prime minister. Zhuangzi refused. He asked the messengers whether a sacrificial turtle would rather be dead and kept in a beautiful box at the royal court, or alive and free, dragging its tail through the mud.When the messengers said the turtle would prefer to be alive in the mud, Zhuangzi told them to leave. He preferred freedom and an ordinary life to wealth, power and official status.In the Zhuangzi, the text associated with the philosopher and his followers, his criticism of rewards and punishments challenged both Legalism and Confucianism. Legalist governments relied heavily on strict laws and harsh punishments, while Confucian systems could use social praise, shame and duty to shape behavior. Zhuangzi saw both approaches as ways of controlling people from the outside.For him, true learning and living in harmony with the Dao required an inner change. It had to happen naturally, through ziran, or spontaneous and natural action, rather than through forced obedience.At the center of Zhuangzi’s argument is a simple psychological idea: when you offer a reward for doing something, you can make the person see the activity itself as less valuable.If a child needs a gold star before they will read a book, the child may begin to think that reading is the work and the gold star is the real reward. If an adult behaves honestly only because they fear punishment, they may not have developed integrity. They may simply have learned how to avoid getting caught.This idea has a connection with modern psychology. In 1971, psychologist Edward Deci conducted experiments at the University of Rochester involving people solving puzzles. His research suggested that when people were paid to do an activity they already enjoyed, their interest in the activity could decrease after the payment was removed. The external reward could change something that was once enjoyable into something that felt like work.Punishment can work in a similar way. It can stop unwanted behavior through fear without changing the person's deeper understanding or values. Once the threat of punishment disappears, the old behavior may return.For Zhuangzi, education was not about filling people with forced information or training them to obey rules. It was about allowing a person's natural qualities, or de, to develop. He considered rewards and punishments the “lowest form” of education because they assume people have no internal direction and therefore must be pushed toward good behavior from the outside.Zhuangzi’s warning remains relevant in modern institutions.In the workplace, companies have long used performance bonuses, rankings and performance improvement plans to encourage employees to work harder. But these systems can sometimes produce compliance instead of creativity. In Drive, author Daniel Pink argues that external rewards can narrow people's attention and weaken intrinsic motivation, especially when work requires creativity, judgment and complex problem-solving.A company that wants innovation may therefore face a contradiction. If employees are mainly focused on bonuses or avoiding punishment, they may become less willing to experiment, make mistakes or take intelligent risks. They may focus on meeting the measured target instead of finding the best solution.The same problem can appear in schools. When students become heavily focused on grades and test scores, they may learn how to pass exams rather than develop a lasting interest in the subject. Short-term memorization can become more important than deep understanding. Once the exam is over and the grade has been recorded, much of the information may quickly be forgotten.Seeing education through Zhuangzi’s perspective does not mean removing all rules, structure or standards. Instead, it means changing where motivation comes from.A good teacher, mentor or leader creates conditions in which the work itself has meaning, learning feels valuable, and improvement matters more than simply avoiding failure. When people understand why something matters and are given room to develop mastery, they are more likely to act from within rather than because someone is watching them.Centuries after Zhuangzi chose the freedom of the mud over the comfort of the royal court, his central idea still carries weight: a system that depends completely on threats and rewards to make people act has already revealed that it cannot inspire them from within.
Article Summary: Zhuangzi was an ancient Chinese philosopher who championed freedom, natural living, and inner wisdom over forced rules and external rewards. He considered rewards and punishments the “lowest form” of education because they assume people have no internal direction and therefore must be pushed toward good behavior from the outside.

Article Title: Video: 2 injured after gunman opens fire near New York subway station
Article Text:
NYPD said a 20-year-old and a 31-year-old man were injured in the Bronx shooting.

Two men were injured after a gunman opened fire near a busy subway station in New York City's Bronx on Thursday evening, NY police said.The shooting happened at around 6 p.m. outside the West Farms Square-E Tremont Avenue subway station. Surveillance footage from the area showed a man wearing a white hoodie walking towards a plaza before firing several shots in the direction of a group gathered near a shop.Video from the scene also captured people fleeing as the gunman escaped. One man was seen tumbling over a bench and rolling onto the pavement, although it was not immediately clear whether he had been hit by gunfire.According to the New York Police Department (NYPD), a 20-year-old man was shot in the leg, while a 31-year-old man suffered a gunshot wound to the buttocks.Both victims were taken to St. Barnabas Hospital, where they were reported to be in stable condition.Police have not confirmed whether the two injured men were the intended targets or were caught in the gunfire by chance.The suspect fled the scene after the shooting. No arrests had been announced as of Thursday night, and the investigation remains ongoing.
Article Summary: The shooting happened at around 6 p.m. outside the West Farms Square-E Tremont Avenue subway station in New York City's Bronx. A 20-year-old man was shot in the leg, while a 31-year old man suffered a gunshot wound to the buttocks. Both victims were taken to St Barnabas Hospital, where they were reported to be in stable condition.

Article Title: PhD student Vikram Mubayi found dead in lake after going missing on solo hiking trip in US
Article Text:
UC Santa Barbara PhD student Vikram Mubayi was found dead after going missing during a solo hike in California's Inyo National Forest.

Vikram Mubayi, a chemical engineering PhD student at the University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB), was found dead on August 3 in California's Inyo National Forest, two days after he went missing during a solo hiking trip in the Big Pine Lakes area.According to local reports, Mubayi last contacted his family on the evening of August 1 before a search operation was launched by Inyo County Search & Rescue.Authorities later recovered Mubayi's body from Big Pine Lakes, and officials said the circumstances surrounding his death remain under investigation, with no indication of foul play.Born and raised in Hong Kong, Mubayi was described by his family as an experienced hiker.In a post on Reddit, his sibiling urged people to inform if someone had seen Vikram. "My brother Vikram is 6’3, 170lbs, dark hair, and has been out of contact since 8.30pm yesterday in the big pine lakes area in the eastern sierra, specifically around agassiz col. Have attached a link to his route here strava.com/routes/3516945857263630584. Did anyone happen to see him along the way? he last sent an update 8.37PM PST from the following coordinates: 37.10942° N, 118.52428° W" the post said."He’s a fairly experienced hiker and we think that he reached a reasonably easy part of the route, so would have expected him back by now. his car is still at the trailhead. So sorry if this is not the right place to post. can post somewhere else if there’s a better place," it added.The official confirmation is yet to come from the authorities.
Article Summary: Vikram Mubayi, a chemical engineering PhD student at the University of California, Santa Barbara, was found dead on August 3 in California's Inyo National Forest. The circumstances surrounding his death remain under investigation, with no indication of foul play.

Article Title: Iran President met a 'voice in the dark', isn't sure it was Mojtaba Khamenei: Report
Article Text:
Iran president says he heard a voice, not saw a face in secret Khamenei meeting

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think the speculation regarding Khamenei health and whereabouts is justified? Yes, there are valid concerns. No, it’s just baseless rumors. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian was reportedly taken to a secret location in Tehran and granted only a brief meeting with a man introduced as Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, according to Iran International.The reported encounter, conducted inside a dark, tinted-window vehicle, has fuelled fresh questions over the secrecy surrounding Iran's leadership.According to the report, Pezeshkian was unable to see the man seated beside him and later questioned whether the voice he heard had indeed belonged to the country's new supreme leader.Their account of what they described as the only known meeting between the president and Iran's third supreme leader differs markedly from Pezeshkian's public version of events.Speaking at a gathering of trade association representatives in mid-May, Pezeshkian said he had spent two and a half hours with the new leader in what he described as a "cordial atmosphere."However, the report said that the meeting lasted only a few minutes, after which the president was asked to leave.According to the report, the meeting took place only after Pezeshkian repeatedly sought an audience with the supreme leader and threatened to resign.They said the leader's office agreed to the meeting under pressure but informed the president that, unlike previous practice, he would not be received at the supreme leader's official residence.Instead, Pezeshkian's security team reportedly took him to an undisclosed location in Tehran, where he was escorted from his vehicle into the back seat of a dark, tinted-window commercial car. The report claimed the supreme leader was already inside, but the vehicle was kept dark enough that the two men could not see each other. They also alleged that Khamenei's security personnel did not allow a handshake, and the conversation took place entirely by voice.The reported arrangement left Pezeshkian feeling humiliated, as per the report.Officials in the president's office told Iran International that he later questioned whether the person beside him had actually been the supreme leader, as he had only heard a voice during the brief meeting.Pezeshkian had earlier acknowledged that communicating with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei is "very difficult.""It is very difficult to communicate with him at the moment, but in any case, his presence is a very great source of strength for us so that we can continue," Pezeshkian said.Mojtaba Khamenei has continued to issue written statements, but his absence from public view since assuming Iran's top leadership has fuelled speculation about his relationship with senior officials and his whereabouts. Nearly five months after the Assembly of Experts selected him to succeed his father as supreme leader, no audio recording or video of him has been released.The prolonged silence has also drawn attention in Iran's state-aligned media. On Sunday, the Hamshahri newspaper's website published a video claiming that foreign intelligence agencies could use advanced acoustic analysis of audio recordings, including background noise, electrical grid frequency signatures and vocal characteristics, to identify the leader's location or assess his physical condition.The claims appeared to deepen, rather than dispel, speculation surrounding Khamenei's status.Conflicting assessments have also emerged internationally. Three weeks ago, US President Donald Trump said there was a "90 percent" chance that Mojtaba Khamenei had been killed, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has more recently said the Iranian leader is alive.
Article Summary: Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian was reportedly taken to a secret location in Tehran and granted only a brief meeting with a man introduced as Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. The reported encounter, conducted inside a dark, tinted-window vehicle, has fuelled fresh questions over the secrecy surrounding Iran's leadership.

Article Title: Watch: Scared Thailand school students duck under desks as gunshots ring out; 8 dead
Article Text:
Video shows Thailand students hiding under desks during school shooting (Image: X@/CatchUpFeed)

At least eight people were killed on Friday after a student opened fire at a school in Thailand before turning the gun on himself, a national police official said.The gunman first shot and killed his grandparents at their home before opening fire at the school.The student fired 26 rounds, while another 34 rounds of ammunition were recovered from the scene, according to a police statement.Videos from the scene showed students ducking under their desks as gunshots could be heard in the background.The shooting took place at Debsirin Nonthaburi School in Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi province, northwest of Bangkok. Police identified the shooter as a student.Lt Col Dechrapee Kongdee, commander of the Nonthaburi Provincial Police, confirmed the casualties to Reuters and said the suspected gunman had died by suicide.He said those injured included one teacher and three students.An 18-year-old student said he initially mistook the sound of gunfire for firecrackers going off or someone banging an object."I didn't think ⁠it was a gun at first," he was quoted as saying by Reuters. "There were many shots: bang bang bang. Then it went quiet. Then it started again."According to district authorities, the school had around 3,100 students and 147 teachers enrolled during the 2025 academic year.The latest incident comes months after a teacher was killed and a student injured in a separate shooting at a school in Hat Yai district in southern Thailand in February.
Article Summary: Shooting took place at Debsirin Nonthaburi School in Bang Kruai district, northwest of Bangkok. Gunman first shot and killed his grandparents at their home before opening fire at the school. Video shows students ducking under their desks as gunshots can be heard in background.

Article Title: Exiled Bangladeshi cricket star Shakib Al Hasan willing to return, face murder trial if safety assured
Article Text:
Bangladesh cricket star Shakib Al Hasan, an exiled ally of ousted PM Sheikh Hasina, says he is ready to return home and face trial on murder charges if the government guarantees his security.

Bangladesh cricket Shakib Al Hasan has said he is willing to return home and face criminal proceedings against him if the government guarantees his safety, according to an exclusive interview with Reuters.Shakib has been living in exile in the United States since former prime minister Sheikh Hasina was ousted in a student-led uprising in August 2024. The former Bangladesh captain, who was also an Awami League lawmaker under Hasina, has not returned home since.“If I get the clearance from the government that my security will be ensured, I am happy to go back, face the court trial and everything that's needed to be done,” Shakib told Reuters by phone from Sri Lanka.He said he believed the allegations against him were baseless and wanted the opportunity to return and defend himself in court. Shakib said he was also keen to speak with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman about his return.Shakib is facing two active cases in Bangladesh. One concerns the alleged killing of a protester during the 2024 uprising, while another was filed by anti-corruption authorities. He said the murder case was filed on a day when he was playing a match in Toronto.Shakib also said his bank accounts had been frozen for around 18 months while investigations continued. He has not appointed a defence lawyer in the murder case, according to Reuters.His political links remain a major obstacle to his return. Shakib defended his decision to appear virtually at a press conference with Hasina in Delhi this week, saying he had only called for peace and progress in Bangladesh. He said he had no intention of distancing himself from Hasina or the Awami League to facilitate his return.The Rahman government, however, has rejected any suggestion of special treatment. His press secretary A.A.M. Saleh told Reuters that Shakib was facing the consequences of his association with the former government and that Bangladeshi law applied equally to everyone.“Shakib Al Hasan is an accused person, and he must surrender before the courts of Bangladesh to face the judicial process,” Saleh said.Shakib said he had previously tried to return. In late 2024, he boarded a flight home after receiving assurances that he would be protected, but was reportedly instructed to turn around while the plane was in transit. He returned to New York after landing in Dubai.A subsequent attempt also failed after he posted a birthday message for Hasina, which authorities cited as a reason for preventing his entry, he said.Despite the political and legal uncertainty, Shakib has not retired from international cricket. He said he wants to play a farewell series at home and hopes to represent Bangladesh at the 2027 ODI World Cup, although he acknowledged that he cannot continue indefinitely.“I am feeling good, still enjoying the game, playing well also,” Shakib told Reuters. “But ... age is not on my side at this moment, so I cannot wait for too long.”The cricketer also said he has not seen his parents in Bangladesh for two years and that the prolonged separation had been difficult for his family.
Article Summary: Bangladesh cricket star Shakib Al Hasan says he is willing to return home and face criminal proceedings against him if the government guarantees his safety. Shakib has been living in exile in the United States since former prime minister Sheikh Hasina was ousted in a student-led uprising in August 2024. The former Bangladesh captain, who was also an Awami League lawmaker under Hasina, has not returned home since.

Article Title: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan & Turkey sign 'Mecca' pact for mutual defence; India reacts
Article Text:
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan each bring distinct strategic strengths to the partnership.

Deal amid turbulent West Asia

3 distinct strategic strengths

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey Friday signed a trilateral defence agreement aimed at strengthening their collective security as the conflict involving Iran continues to fuel instability across the West Asia.The agreement was signed following a joint defence summit attended by Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani prime minister Shehbaz Sharif, who attended after performing the Umrah pilgrimage in the city.According to Pakistan's foreign ministry, the pact is "guided by the longstanding historical ties among the three states, based on the enduring bonds of brotherhood and Islamic solidarity that unite them, and building upon their shared strategic interests and longstanding defence cooperation".The agreement is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three would be regarded as an attack on all, they said in a joint statement.The Pakistani ministry said the agreement reflects "the three states’ shared commitment to further strengthening their collective security and to promoting peace, security, and stability in the region and beyond, in pursuit of a secure and prosperous future."Also read: Evening news wrap: CBI chargesheet alleges NTA's own experts leaked NEET-UG, MEA rejects US criticism of of FCRA Bill & more It added that "The agreement is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression, and stipulates that any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all."Meanwhile, India reacted to the development, saying "developments were closely watched".Responding to reports on the agreement, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said: “The pact between the three countries is, again, a development that we are closely following, and we will keep you updated on that.”The deal comes as Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries continue to face missile attacks and disruptions to energy shipments amid the ongoing conflict involving Iran and its regional allies. The war escalated after the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran on February 28, triggering a wider regional crisis.A Turkish official said the agreement was purely defensive, was not aimed at any particular country and remained open to participation by other regional nations. The official also said it would not replace any existing bilateral or multilateral security arrangements.Analysts said the summit carried significant geopolitical weight at a time of growing uncertainty in the region."The political symbolism of the summit is significant. Three of the Muslim world's most influential states are convening at a moment of heightened uncertainty, demonstrating a growing willingness among regional and middle powers to coordinate more closely on security matters," Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Saudi-based Gulf Research Center, told new agency Reuters."If institutionalised and translated into concrete cooperation, the trilateral framework could strengthen the three countries' collective diplomatic and defense weight while contributing to the emergence of a more regionally driven security architecture," Sager added.Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan each bring distinct strategic strengths to the partnership. Turkey has Nato's second-largest military, Saudi Arabia is one of the world's biggest oil exporters and custodian of Islam's holiest sites, while Pakistan is the only Muslim-majority country with nuclear weapons.The agreement follows months of discussions on expanding regional security cooperation. Earlier this year, Turkish foreign minister Hakan Fidan had said Ankara supported a broader regional security platform to promote stability.Experts believe the pact builds on long-standing military ties among the three countries. Pakistan has trained Saudi security forces for decades, while Turkey and Pakistan have cooperated on defence equipment and military training. Saudi Arabia also signed a major deal in 2023 to purchase Turkish drones.Mansoor Ahmed of the Australian National University's Strategic and Defence Studies Centre said Pakistan and Turkey could contribute advanced defence manufacturing capabilities, while Saudi Arabia could provide financial and technological investment.He added, however, that the new agreement was unlikely to include a nuclear component because Pakistan's nuclear deterrent remains focused on India.Pakistan has also expanded its military presence in Saudi Arabia in recent months by deploying thousands of troops, fighter aircraft, drones and air defence systems. It has simultaneously pursued broader security partnerships with Gulf countries, including talks with Kuwait on an expanded defence arrangement linked to energy cooperation and investment.
Article Summary: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed a trilateral defence agreement. The agreement is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression. An armed attack against any of the three would be regarded as an attack on all. The deal comes as Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries continue to face missile attacks.

Article Title: Trump’s Iran ‘victory’ within reach? Tehran raises stakes over Hormuz
Article Text:
Trump’s Iran strategy faces tough Hormuz test

US president Donald Trump had been preparing to declare victory in the war with Iran if Tehran agreed to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz. He had also privately signalled to senior aides that he was willing to walk away without securing a nuclear deal, US officials said to the Wall Street Journal.However, that scaled-back objective has become more difficult after Iran on Saturday made its most extensive demands yet for restoring the free flow of traffic through the strategic waterway, including billions of dollars in US payments, the withdrawal of American troops from the region and an end to the US naval blockade.Trump has repeatedly threatened a major escalation of the US bombing campaign against Iran, only to later pull back from such plans. However, the latest turmoil in negotiations suggests Tehran is preparing for a prolonged and increasingly difficult conflict.In recent days, Trump told reporters that he was prepared to launch what he described as the biggest military attack since World War II, but said US allies had persuaded him to reconsider. He also maintained that a deal with Iran was “imminent”, although no agreement has materialised so far.On Friday, Trump appeared to suggest on social media that the US had already secured victory in the conflict even without a nuclear agreement, sharing an article titled “Donald Trump Won the Iran War.”Vice president JD Vance, meanwhile, told Fox News that Washington would continue to pressure Tehran to make long-term changes in its relationship with the United States.“And if not, that’s fine, too, we’re just going to keep on applying the pressure we can apply, and getting as much oil and gas out of the Middle East so that Americans can enjoy lower gas and energy prices," Vance said.“We’re in the middle of the game,” he added.Iran’s ability to disrupt traffic through the Strait of Hormuz with sporadic missile and drone attacks has given Tehran significant leverage, slowing commercial shipping and affecting global oil markets. Trump has repeatedly said in recent weeks that the strait was fully open, but those claims have so far proved premature.Tehran, which closed the waterway after the war began in February, has insisted that American warships not be allowed to pass through and has sought to collect revenue from commercial vessels. Washington, however, has said it will not accept Iranian restrictions or tolls, US officials said.Prospects for an agreement appeared to weaken further over the weekend after the United Arab Emirates said Iran had launched a missile attack on one of its ships. A senior Iranian official also outlined a series of demands that Tehran says must be met before traffic through the strait can resume.Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said the US would have to permanently end the war, lift its naval blockade, withdraw its forces, end all sanctions, release Iran’s frozen assets, pay war reparations, stop threats and insults, and halt military action against Iran’s militia allies in the region before Tehran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, according to a report by state news agency IRNA.
Article Summary: Donald Trump had been preparing to declare victory in the war with Iran if Tehran agreed to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz. He had also privately signalled to senior aides that he was willing to walk away without securing a nuclear deal. Iran on Saturday made its most extensive demands yet for restoring the free flow of traffic through the strategic waterway, including billions of dollars in US payments.

Article Title: '51 years of bad behaviour': Trump takes swipe at Iran with 'no money' claims
Article Text:
The post comes as Trump has repeatedly argued that Iran’s economy has been weakened by years of international sanctions, regional conflicts and what he has described as the Iranian leadership’s confrontational policies.

Trump calls Iran's currency 'trash'

US President Donald Trump on Sunday criticised Iran in a post on his social media platform Truth Social, sharing a graphic titled “Iran has NO MONEY” and blaming the country’s economic decline on what he described as “51 years of bad behaviour. ”The post, which was accompanied by a chart showing the sharp depreciation of the Iranian rial against the US dollar, appeared to be Trump’s latest public attack on Tehran amid heightened tensions between the United States and Iran.The image shared by Trump claimed that 1 million Iranian rials was worth about $1.11 in early 2025, but had fallen to around $0.53 by the third quarter of 2026. A downward-sloping graph tracked the currency’s decline across several quarters, ending with the caption “Currency is Trash” next to a trash-bin icon.The graphic was designed to suggest that Iran’s currency had lost more than half of its value over the period shown, portraying the country as being in severe economic distress. Trump did not provide additional commentary beyond the caption “51 years of bad behavior!”, which appeared above the image on Truth Social.The post comes as Trump has repeatedly argued that Iran’s economy has been weakened by years of international sanctions, regional conflicts and what he has described as the Iranian leadership’s confrontational policies.His administration has continued to maintain pressure on Tehran through sanctions and military deployments in the Middle East.Iran’s currency has experienced prolonged depreciation over the past several years, driven by inflation, sanctions-related pressures, reduced foreign investment and instability in foreign exchange markets. Economists have long pointed to structural weaknesses in Iran’s economy, although the specific exchange-rate figures circulated on social media often depend on which official or parallel-market rate is used.Trump’s post also comes against the backdrop of the ongoing US-Iran confrontation that has intensified in recent weeks.Washington and Tehran have been engaged in escalating military and diplomatic tensions, including US operations targeting Iranian-linked assets and increased American military deployments in the region. The developments have raised concerns over a wider regional conflict, even as backchannel diplomatic efforts involving Gulf states and Oman have reportedly continued in an attempt to prevent further escalation.
Article Summary: The post was accompanied by a chart showing the sharp depreciation of the Iranian rial against the US dollar. The image claimed that 1 million Iranian rials was worth about $1.11 in early 2025, but had fallen to around $0.53 by the third quarter of 2026. The graphic was designed to suggest that Iran’s currency had lost more than half of its value.

Article Title: No more strikes on Iran? Trump says US going 'low key', stresses economic pressure over military op
Article Text:
Trump claims that Iran is facing economic crisis as they have 'no money'

US President Donald Trump said Sunday that the US is taking a low-key approach towards Iran and is not currently looking to launch a new military offensive, even as tensions over the Strait of Hormuz continue.“We are low keying it,” Trump told Axios in a brief phone call, adding that the US was only “semi-negotiating” with Iran while watching its worsening economic situation.“We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money,” Trump said.Trump said Iran was “in very bad shape” economically and that the US naval blockade has worsened the crisis. He also said lower oil prices, at slightly above $75 a barrel, meant American consumers were facing less economic pain from the conflict.“It will work out. It always works out. It’s like a chess game,” Trump further said.His remarks come as talks on an agreement involving Iran, Oman and the US to reopen the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled. Iran has issued additional demands for reopening the key shipping route, including an end to the US naval blockade and withdrawal of US forces from around Iran.Trump did not issue any new military threats against Iran in the interview. Although last week, US officials had indicated that he was considering resuming major military operations against the country. However, another WSJ report claimed that Trump might be willing to end Iran war even without the nuclear deal with agreement on reopening Hormuz.Read more: Backed into a corner? Trump ready to end Iran war without nuclear deal – report
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump says the US is taking a low-key approach towards Iran. He said the US was only ‘semi-negotiating’ with Iran while watching its worsening economic situation. Trump did not issue any new military threats against Iran in the interview.

Article Title: Florida couple visited Greece for the first time in 2024; two years later, they retired early and moved into a $461,000 home bought sight unseen
Article Text:
Both worked in hospitality and had a comfortable life but as retirement loomed they started to think about living abroad.

From Florida to Greece

A holiday that altered their plans

Selling their life in Florida

Beginning again from the ground up

Greek way of life education

Understanding the local culture

A new chapter for Greece

Two years ago, Greece was just a vacation destination for Jeffrey Davidson and Walter Zak. Today it is home. A Florida couple who spent three decades building a life near Orlando decided to retire early and move to the Peloponnese after one trip to Greece changed their plans for the future. Their story, reported by CNN Newsource, is an unusual case of how a vacation can lead to a total lifestyle change. Now living in the coastal area of Akrata, the couple has swapped Florida's theme-park vibe for ancient ruins, seaside views and a slower pace of everyday life. They bought a house in the village of Platanos for 400,000 euros, or about $461,000 US, without ever seeing it in person before they bought it.Jeffrey, 62, and Walter, 57, met 32 years ago and lived most of their adult lives together in Florida. Both worked in hospitality and had a comfortable life but as retirement loomed they started to think about living abroad. It was no flight from the United States. Instead they wanted to experience another culture and create a different kind of daily life. Their first choice was the Caribbean island of St. Martin, where they used to go and have a great time. " But the expense of relocating there, and the fear of hurricanes, made them change their minds.For the couple, Greece had not been a leading point for possible retirement locations. That changed in 2024 when the couple visited the country to mark their 30th anniversary. The trip was two weeks of exploring Greece, including a 10-day cruise around the Greek islands and a visit to Thessaloniki, the birthplace of Walter’s grandfather. The trip gave them an opportunity to experience the culture, people and pace of life of the country. Instead of deciding to move immediately, they spent the next year investigating whether a permanent move was a realistic option. Walter dug into the financial and legal requirements and found that they could potentially qualify for Greece’s Golden Visa program through a qualifying real estate investment. The couple took the plunge about a year after their trip.The decision was more than two plane tickets. Jeffrey sold his Corvette a week after agreeing to retire early and move. The couple also sold their three-story townhome in Florida and scaled back greatly on the amount of belongings they planned to bring with them. They viewed a few properties, and settled on Akrata, in the Peloponnese, for its milder climate and proximity to the sea. Then came one of the biggest leaps of faith, buying their new home without seeing it in person.The Platanos property was listed at €400,000 fully furnished with one bedroom main house and a separate one bedroom guest apartment. The property also has views over the Gulf of Corinth.When the couple finally landed in Greece in April, they had only 10 suitcases with them. The rest of their stuff came later in a shipping container. The first few weeks were filled with practical challenges. From obtaining mobile phones and internet service, to purchasing a car, to figuring out everyday necessities like where to get propane. These challenges were not viewed as reasons to regret the move, but rather as part of the learning process. “Every day there’s new things to learn, from local services to how businesses operate. They thought it was easier to make the transition because they relocated while they were still young enough to adapt.One of the biggest adjustments has been getting used to the slower pace of life in Greece. The couple found that dinner was usually served much later than they were used to in Florida. Locals usually eat later in the evening, so if you go to a restaurant around 7 p.m. you will probably find the dining room nearly empty. They have adapted to the mesimeri, the traditional afternoon break when many businesses close for several hours. Sundays can be particularly quiet with many establishments closed for the day. At first, the differences made Greece feel like a foreign place. But the slower pace gradually became something they valued most.The couple purposely selected a city with relatively few foreigners because they wanted to live Greek, not replicate their American lifestyle abroad. They have begun learning Greek and have just finished a week-long language course. They have struggled to learn the language, but they keep practicing whenever they get the chance. English is widely spoken, especially by the younger generation, which has helped them to cope with daily life. They have befriended local residents and become regulars at nearby restaurants where they enjoy long meals and a relaxed approach to dining.Four months later, Jeffrey and Walter were still acclimating to their new environment, but they already felt the decision had paid off. Their house is a quiet base from which to explore nearby towns and cities, including Athens. Friends and family have also visited, giving the couple a chance to spend time with loved ones without the hectic schedules they had grown accustomed to in their previous life in Florida. They don’t intend to leave the United States permanently, at least for now. After decades in Florida, the couple seems to have found what they were looking for: a quieter place to live, a new culture to embrace and the freedom to slow down and enjoy retirement on their own terms.Image Courtesy: CNN Newsource
Article Summary: Two years ago, Greece was just a vacation destination for Jeffrey Davidson and Walter Zak. The couple has swapped Florida's theme-park vibe for ancient ruins, seaside views and a slower pace of everyday life. They bought a house in the village of Platanos for 400,000 euros, or about $461,000 US, without ever seeing it in person.

Article Title: In 1987, Orlando put 1,200 acres of constructed wetlands to work cleaning reclaimed water; the system now polishes about 5.11 billion gallons a year
Article Text:
Orlando Wetlands

Clearing 200,000 cubic yards of organic sediment

How aquatic plants remove nutrients from municipal effluent

Historical wet prairie roots of the St. Johns River basin

Long-term maintenance keeps water polishing effective

In 1987, Orlando put 1,200 acres of constructed wetlands to work cleaning reclaimed water. Today, the system treats about 5.11 billion gallons of water each year.However, keeping this large natural filtration system working efficiently requires regular land management. As aquatic plants grow, absorb extra nitrogen and phosphorus, and eventually die and decay, a thick layer of organic muck slowly builds up on the bottom of the marsh. When this sediment becomes too thick, it can slow water flow and cause stored nutrients to return to the water. This makes periodic earthmoving work necessary to keep the system working properly.According to operational records published by the City of Orlando Water Reclamation Division, city crews carry out large renovation projects, known as demucking, to remove the built-up organic material and restore the marsh's original ability to clean the water.Ongoing research and water-flow monitoring help the city determine when specific areas of the 1,200-acre complex need maintenance. Once an area is chosen, operators separate it from the rest of the system, close the incoming water lines and completely drain the marsh cell.Heavy construction equipment then moves onto the dry basin floor. Workers scrape away dead vegetation and about 18 inches of compacted organic muck.City records show that individual renovation projects cover about 100 acres on average and remove around 200,000 cubic yards of organic sediment during each cycle.After the heavy equipment finishes, workers level the ground and replant native aquatic plants. These species are selected because they can absorb nutrients effectively and provide good habitat for wildlife. Important plants used during restoration include giant bulrush, pickerelweed and duck potato.Once the area has been replanted, water gates are opened again. Reclaimed water from Orlando's municipal treatment facilities can then flow through the restored marsh cells. The city first used this demucking method in August 2002, after about 15 years of continuous operation. Similar renovation projects have since been carried out in different parts of the property to keep the wetland's water-cleaning performance stable.The main biological process depends on a continuous natural cycle that cleans reclaimed water before it leaves the facility. When treated water enters the 1,200-acre wetland, aquatic plants remove extra nitrogen and phosphorus from the water through their growth.As the plants grow, they take in these dissolved nutrients and store them in their tissues. But this natural growth also creates the main long-term maintenance problem that makes demucking necessary.When the plants finish their life cycle, they fall into the shallow water and slowly decay. Their remains collect on the bottom and form a thick layer of organic muck. Over many years, this layer becomes deeper and denser.If the sediment is not removed, it can slow the movement of water through the marsh. Nutrients trapped in the organic material can also be released back into the water. At this point, mechanical removal is needed to restore the wetland's ability to filter the water effectively.The land where the Orlando Wetlands is located was historically a wet prairie, a type of freshwater wetland that played an important role in the hydrology of central Florida. Records from the St. Johns River Water Management District describe wet prairies as mostly treeless freshwater wetlands dominated by native grasses, sedges and other plants adapted to soils that remain wet for long periods.The original land was part of the upper St. Johns River basin, a large marshy headwaters region. This basin developed naturally because the St. Johns River has an extremely low slope, dropping only about one inch per mile.Because the land is so flat, water moves very slowly across it. This creates wide, shallow wetlands that can remain wet for much of the year. The original wet prairie was ecologically important because it stored floodwater, filtered nutrients coming from surrounding watersheds and provided habitat for many species of birds, fish and amphibians.By converting former agricultural land back into a functioning artificial marsh in 1987, the City of Orlando restored some of these natural water-management functions while also creating a reliable, low-energy municipal water treatment system.Without regular physical maintenance, constructed wetlands can gradually lose their ability to treat municipal wastewater. The demucking program helps prevent the 1,200-acre artificial marsh from becoming clogged with sediment or becoming a source of nutrient pollution.By regularly draining sections of about 100 acres, removing around 18 inches of decayed organic material, leveling the soil and replanting native species such as giant bulrush and pickerelweed, the city maintains the wetland's ability to move and clean water.The process combines engineering with natural biological processes. This allows the artificial wet prairie to continue polishing about 5.11 billion gallons of reclaimed water each year while also maintaining a stable habitat for local wildlife.
Article Summary: Orlando's 1,200-acre wetland system treats about 5.11 billion gallons of water each year. As aquatic plants grow, absorb extra nitrogen and phosphorus, and eventually die and decay, a thick layer of organic muck slowly builds up. When this sediment becomes too thick, it can slow water flow and cause stored nutrients to return to the water. This makes periodic earthmoving work necessary to keep the system working properly.

Article Title: Florida community fears a radioactive waste pile could threaten thousands living nearby
Article Text:
Image: Amy Green/Inside Climate News

A massive industrial waste stack towers over a historically Black community

Progress Village has lived beside the problem for decades

The concern extends beyond radiation to water and flooding

Scientists have found that phosphogypsum can affect air and water quality

The health question is more complicated than it looks

Florida's phosphate industry faces a much larger waste problem

A community is asking how long the waste can remain part of its landscape

In Progress Village, Florida, a huge mound of industrial waste has become a symbol of a much bigger environmental and public-health debate. The historically Black community sits beside a massive phosphogypsum stack, a structure created from the waste left behind during phosphate fertiliser production.The stack is difficult to miss. The structure covers about 367 acres and is topped by a retention pond containing millions of gallons of water associated with fertiliser production. Residents have spent years questioning whether living so close to the site exposes their families to unacceptable environmental risks.The concerns are particularly serious because phosphogypsum is not simply ordinary industrial waste. It can contain naturally occurring radioactive materials, including uranium, thorium and radium, which are inherited from the phosphate rock used during fertiliser production.Phosphogypsum is produced when phosphate rock is processed to manufacture phosphoric acid, which is then used to make fertiliser. Large quantities of the by-product are generated during the process, leaving companies with a difficult waste-management problem.The US Environmental Protection Agency explains that phosphate ore contains uranium and radium, meaning these radionuclides can remain in phosphogypsum. Radium is particularly important because it decays into radon, a radioactive gas that can increase the risk of lung cancer following prolonged exposure at elevated levels.A 2025 review by Linda Maina, Katarzyna Kiegiel and Grażyna Zakrzewska-Kołtuniewicz, published in Sustainability under the title ‘ Challenges and Strategies for the Sustainable Environmental Management of Phosphogypsum ’, highlighted the wider environmental problems associated with the material. The authors noted that phosphogypsum can contain radionuclides and potentially toxic trace elements, with the composition varying according to the geological source of the phosphate rock.The researchers specifically identified phosphate rock from Florida as having comparatively high concentrations of uranium, thorium and their decay products, reinforcing the need for careful management and monitoring of the resulting waste.The concerns surrounding the stack are inseparable from the history of Progress Village itself. The community was established in the 1950s as a planned neighbourhood for Black residents during a period when racial segregation severely restricted where African Americans could live. Over time, industrial development expanded around the community.Residents later opposed the construction of another phosphogypsum stack in the area during the 1980s. Their objections did not prevent the project from going ahead, and the resulting waste structure eventually became a permanent part of the landscape.Today, residents continue to question whether their community has carried an unfair share of the environmental burden created by the region's phosphate industry. WUSF reported that environmental engineer and Progress Village resident Walter Smith II has worked to raise awareness of the potential health and safety risks facing people living near the industrial facilities.Radiation is only one part of the problem residents worry about. Phosphogypsum stacks are often topped by large retention ponds containing process water. That creates another potential environmental vulnerability, particularly in a state regularly exposed to hurricanes and extreme rainfall.The dangers of poorly contained phosphate-industry wastewater became especially visible in 2021, when a serious leak at the former Piney Point facility in Florida led authorities to evacuate nearby residents and discharge millions of gallons of contaminated water to prevent a potentially larger failure.Progress Village residents therefore face a difficult question: what could happen if a major storm, flooding event or structural failure compromised one of the enormous industrial waste structures surrounding the community?The local environmental advocates have specifically raised concerns about the consequences of a major hurricane striking the area, given the combination of the phosphogypsum stack, its wastewater reservoir and existing flooding vulnerabilities.Research into Florida's phosphogypsum stacks has provided reasons for continued monitoring, although it does not establish that every person living near a stack will develop cancer.The study published in Environmental Monitoring and Assessment measured radon and particulate matter near three large Florida phosphogypsum stacks. The researchers described phosphogypsum as a major source of concern because of its radon emissions and investigated how atmospheric concentrations varied with distance and weather conditions.Water contamination is another issue scientists have investigated. Research titled ‘ Fate and transport of radioactive gypsum stack water entering the Floridan aquifer due to a sinkhole collapse ,’ found that after a 2016 sinkhole beneath Florida phosphogypsum stack allowed contaminated water to enter the underlying aquifer. The research modelled the movement of radioactive stack water through the Floridan aquifer system, highlighting the importance of protecting groundwater around these facilities.These studies do not prove a specific cancer burden in Progress Village. They instead demonstrate why communities near phosphogypsum storage facilities have legitimate reasons to demand environmental monitoring and transparent risk assessments.Radon is a recognised lung-cancer risk, and phosphogypsum can contain radium that produces radon. But the existence of radioactive material near a community does not by itself establish how much radiation or radon each resident receives, nor does it prove that a particular cancer was caused by the stack.Cancer can have many causes, exposure levels differ between individuals, and some diseases can take decades to develop. Determining whether an industrial site has caused an increase in cancer requires long-term epidemiological research alongside reliable exposure measurements.That distinction is important because residents' concerns should not be dismissed, but neither should a potential risk be presented as a proven outcome for every person living nearby.The Progress Village stack is part of a much wider challenge. The 2025 Sustainability review noted that phosphogypsum is generated in enormous quantities worldwide, with global production exceeding 200 million tonnes a year and billions of tonnes already stockpiled. Only a relatively small proportion is currently reused, leaving much of the material in long-term storage.The authors argue that the future of phosphogypsum management could involve a shift away from simply storing the material towards carefully controlled reuse. Potential applications include construction materials, cement, plasterboard, agriculture and land reclamation, although radioactive components and differences in chemical composition mean that safety and regulatory controls remain essential.In other words, the challenge is not simply how to store the waste. It is how to deal with billions of tonnes of material without transferring environmental risks from one place to another.For Progress Village, the issue is deeply personal. The phosphogypsum stack is not an abstract environmental problem located far from homes. It stands beside a community whose residents have watched industrial development reshape the landscape around them for generations. The question now is what happens next.Stronger monitoring of air, water and radiation levels could provide residents with clearer information about actual exposure. Better emergency planning could address the risks posed by hurricanes and flooding. And research into safer ways of managing or reusing phosphogypsum could eventually reduce the need for enormous waste stacks.The experience of Progress Village illustrates why environmental protection is also an issue of community trust. People living beside industrial waste want to know not only what is stored next door, but what the measurable risks are, how those risks are being controlled and who will be responsible if something goes wrong.For a community that has spent decades living in the shadow of a massive waste pile, those answers matter just as much as the mound itself.
Article Summary: Phosphogypsum is produced when phosphate rock is processed to manufacture phosphoric acid, which is then used to make fertiliser. Large quantities of the by-product are generated during the process, leaving companies with a difficult waste-management problem. It can contain naturally occurring radioactive materials, including uranium, thorium and radium, which are inherited from the phosphate rock used during fertiliser production.

Article Title: In 1986, a California city began polishing sewage through constructed marshes; the 307-acre system is now a wildlife sanctuary that has hosted over 300 bird species
Article Text:
50 Million Gallons of Sewage Flow Daily From Mexico Into California Beaches

Decentralized wetlands replace a costly regional plant

How the wetland system treats sewage

Schoenoplectus acutus

From damaged industrial land to wildlife habitat

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that using constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment is a sustainable practice? Yes, absolutely! No, there are better methods. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Recreation and national recognition

In 1986, the Northern California city of Arcata completed an innovative wastewater treatment system that used constructed wetlands to clean sewage while also creating valuable wildlife habitat. The project eventually became part of the Arcata Marsh and Wildlife Sanctuary, a 307-acre natural area that combines wastewater treatment, habitat restoration, recreation and environmental education. Today, the City of Arcata reports that more than 300 bird species have been recorded at the sanctuary, which lies along the Pacific Flyway and provides an important stopover for migratory birds.Arcata's decision to use wetlands for wastewater treatment grew out of strict environmental regulations introduced in the 1970s. At the time, the city's wastewater system discharged treated wastewater into Humboldt Bay. Earlier improvements to the plant had included oxidation ponds in 1958, chlorination facilities in 1968 and dechlorination facilities in 1975. California's Bays and Estuaries Policy then placed tighter limits on wastewater discharges into bays and estuaries. The policy required communities to reduce such discharges unless they could show that the discharge would improve the receiving waters.A regional authority responded by proposing a centralized wastewater treatment plant for communities around Humboldt Bay. According to EPA records, the proposal would have required large pipelines around the bay, including an underwater pipeline beneath an active navigation area. The system would also have required significant energy and operating resources and would have discharged treated wastewater offshore in an area exposed to strong ocean conditions.Arcata instead explored a smaller, decentralized approach using constructed wetlands. The idea was influenced by earlier wastewater aquaculture research in the area. Beginning in the late 1960s, researchers experimented with using partly treated wastewater and seawater to raise young Pacific salmon and trout. These experiments suggested that wastewater could be treated as a useful resource rather than simply as waste.From 1979 to 1982, Arcata carried out pilot studies to test whether constructed freshwater wetlands could treat municipal wastewater. The results showed that wetlands could improve wastewater quality while also supporting biological productivity. Based on the successful experiments, Arcata's wastewater task force concluded that a wetland-based system could provide reliable treatment while offering environmental and recreational benefits. State approval followed in 1983, and the full-scale system was completed in 1986.The Arcata system combines conventional wastewater treatment with natural biological processes. EPA documentation identifies seven main stages: headworks, primary clarification, solids handling, oxidation ponds, treatment marshes, enhancement marshes and final disinfection.First, raw sewage enters the headworks, where screens and grit separators remove large pieces of inorganic material. The wastewater then moves into settling tanks, called primary clarifiers, where suspended solids settle to the bottom. These solids are sent to digesters for further treatment. The remaining liquid flows into oxidation ponds, where it stays for an extended period. Natural biological processes in the ponds remove about 50 percent of the remaining biochemical oxygen demand and suspended solids.The water then enters approximately 7.5 acres of treatment marshes planted with native hardstem bulrush (). Plants and microorganisms in the marsh help remove additional organic matter and suspended solids. After intermediate disinfection, the water moves through 31 acres of enhancement marshes: George Allen Marsh, Robert Gearheart Marsh and Dan Hauser Marsh. Sluice gates and wooden weirs control the flow through these marshes before the water receives final disinfection and is discharged into Humboldt Bay.The wetland plants perform several important functions. Their leaves provide shade, helping limit excessive algae growth and keeping water temperatures lower. Plants and microorganisms also help remove nutrients and break down organic material. Bacteria and fungi living in the wetland sediments contribute to the breakdown of complex substances, while the sediments can hold metals and other materials, reducing their movement through the system.The project also changed a heavily disturbed waterfront into a diverse wetland ecosystem. Before restoration, the area contained an abandoned lumber mill pond, channelized sloughs, pastureland and a closed municipal landfill. The project transformed these disturbed areas into a connected landscape containing freshwater marshes, salt marshes, brackish ponds, tidal sloughs, mudflats and grassy uplands.Several parts of the sanctuary were built by reusing previously disturbed land. Robert Gearheart Marsh was developed on former pastureland, while George Allen Marsh was constructed over an abandoned timber log storage deck. Dan Hauser Marsh was created from a gravel borrow pit used during landfill work. Frank Klopp Lake was also formed from a borrow pit and later became habitat for river otters and diving birds. The closed landfill was reclaimed as Mount Trashmore, a grassy public hill.Early EPA reports recorded more than 200 bird species in the restored area. Today, the City of Arcata reports more than 300 species at the sanctuary, which provides important habitat for shorebirds, waterfowl, raptors and migratory birds.It is also important to distinguish the original treatment project from the sanctuary's present size. The City of Arcata's historical timeline shows that the marsh area expanded over time, reaching 154 acres in 1986 and eventually growing to its current 307 acres through later land acquisitions and restoration projects.Public access was part of the project's long-term vision. Today, the sanctuary includes about five miles of walking and biking trails and an Interpretive Center with educational exhibits and information about the marsh's wildlife, history and wastewater treatment system.The project also received national attention. In 1987, the City of Arcata received recognition through the Ford Foundation for its innovative local government work. EPA records state that the award included $100,000, which helped support development of the Arcata Marsh Interpretive Center.The Arcata Marsh project became an important example of nature-based infrastructure. Instead of treating wastewater and environmental restoration as separate goals, Arcata combined them in one system. The result was infrastructure that met wastewater treatment needs while also restoring damaged land, creating wildlife habitat, supporting education and research, and providing a public recreational space. The project demonstrated how a municipal utility could become part of a larger urban ecosystem rather than simply being a piece of industrial infrastructure.
Article Summary: Arcata Marsh and Wildlife Sanctuary is a 307-acre natural area that combines wastewater treatment, habitat restoration, recreation and environmental education. More than 300 bird species have been recorded at the sanctuary, which lies along the Pacific Flyway and provides an important stopover for migratory birds.

Article Title: Utah wildfire: 2 helicopter pilots confirmed dead after crash while battling blaze
Article Text:
This undated photo provided by the U.S. Forest Service on Friday, Aug. 7, 2026, shows the Widemouth 2 wildfire burning near Richfield, Utah. (U.S. Forest Service/Fishlake National Forest via AP)

Pilots confirmed dead after crews reach crash site

Massive Utah wildfire continues to spread

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that more action should be taken to prevent helicopter crashes during firefighting efforts? Yes, absolutely. No, risks are part of the job. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Deadly wildfire season hits US West

Two helicopter pilots who crashed while fighting a wildfire in Utah have been confirmed dead, officials said Saturday, a day after their Sikorsky S-64 Skycrane went down while battling the massive blaze.The helicopter was among several aircraft deployed to fight the Widemouth 2 fire in Fishlake National Forest when it crashed Friday morning near Richfield, about 160 miles south of Salt Lake City.Officials initially said emergency crews could not reach the crash site because of dangerous fire conditions. Crews entered the area Saturday and confirmed the deaths, according to the Sevier County sheriff and coroner.The pilots were employed by Helicopter Transport Services, which was contracted by the US Forest Service. Their identities have not been released.The crash also sparked a new fire that eventually connected with the existing blaze, authorities said.The Widemouth 2 fire has burned more than 114,600 acres, or nearly 179 square miles, and was 24% contained as of Saturday. The blaze has grown rapidly amid hot, dry and windy conditions.More than 600 firefighters have been battling the fire, which has prompted evacuations and destroyed at least six structures.The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the helicopter crash. Investigators were headed to the area and are expected to examine the wreckage once conditions allow.Officials said determining the cause of the crash could take a year or more.The Utah crash came as wildfires continued to spread across several western US states.In Oregon, 47-year-old bulldozer operator Jason Ensign was killed Thursday while working for a timber company as the Wrights Spring fire rapidly expanded and cut off his escape route.The fire had burned more than 30 square miles by Friday and remained uncontained amid extremely hot and dry conditions.Other major fires were also burning in Washington, while a wildfire in British Columbia forced more than 20,000 people to evacuate.
Article Summary: The pilots were employed by Helicopter Transport Services, which was contracted by the US Forest Service. The Widemouth 2 fire has burned more than 114,600 acres, or nearly 179 square miles, and was 24% contained as of Saturday. The crash also sparked a new fire that eventually connected with the existing blaze.

Article Title: In the 1990s, New York chose wetlands over conventional storm sewers on Staten Island; the Bluebelt strategy saved taxpayers $80 million in infrastructure costs
Article Text:
New York City The City of New York Mayor Michael R. Bloomberg Wetlands Strategy

Combining green and grey city infrastructure

Legislative mandates and site restoration targets

Tackling nitrogen runoff and climate surges

In the 1990s, New York chose wetlands over conventional storm sewers on Staten Island; the Bluebelt strategy saved taxpayers $80 million in infrastructure costs.
