Instead of laying miles of underground concrete pipes, the city preserved and restored natural streams, ponds, and freshwater marshes to direct rainwater safely into surrounding bays.The financial and environmental success of the Staten Island Bluebelt model provided the blueprint for water management across New York City. The city’s overarching framework, outlined in the New York City Wetlands Strategy and the PlaNYC 2011 Waterways plan, officially incorporated natural habitats into the municipal infrastructure toolkit alongside conventional treatment facilities.According to figures published in the New York City Wetlands Strategy, urban expansion over the past century wiped out more than 90 per cent of New York City’s freshwater wetlands and roughly 85 per cent of coastal wetlands across the New York-New Jersey Harbor Estuary. Hundreds of miles of natural stream corridors were paved over, buried in underground pipes, or cut off from their natural floodplains.Despite these losses, important ecosystems survived, particularly in Staten Island, the Upper East River, Western Long Island Sound, and Jamaica Bay. Jamaica Bay remains one of the largest tidal wetland systems in the region, serving as a vital stopover on the Atlantic Flyway for over 325 bird species and supporting more than 100 fish species.The municipal planning framework detailed in the PlaNYC 2011 Waterways document established a dual approach to managing runoff, combining grey engineering with green infrastructure.Grey infrastructure relies on concrete storage tanks, pumping stations, sewer mains, and centralized treatment plants. By 2011, New York City operated 14 wastewater treatment facilities handling 1.1 billion gallons of sewage every day during dry weather, following more than $6 billion in municipal harbor water-quality investments since 2002.However, dry-weather capacity did not solve combined sewer overflows (CSOs). In older municipal networks where rainwater and sewage share the same pipes, heavy downpours overwhelm treatment plants, causing direct discharges of untreated wastewater into local waterways. Although the city raised its CSO capture rate from 30 per cent in 1980 to more than 72 per cent by 2010, an estimated 30 billion gallons of CSOs still entered harbor waters annually.To address this volume, the city launched its Green Infrastructure Plan in 2010, committing $1.5 billion over 20 years to capture stormwater at ground level before it enters the sewer system. Municipal evaluations projected that pairing green absorption areas with targeted grey construction would cut CSO volumes by 40 per cent while saving ratepayers over $2 billion compared to building grey infrastructure alone.Major grey engineering investments remained central to the strategy, including large CSO detention facilities at Spring Creek, Paerdegat Basin, and Flushing Bay to store excess rainwater during peak storm events.Local Law 31 of 2009 legally obligated the city to formulate a comprehensive strategy to conserve, protect, restore, and expand wetlands and adjacent buffer zones, setting a goal of no net loss of wetland area.While federal and state legislation protected large tidal wetlands and freshwater areas larger than 12.4 acres, smaller freshwater marshes remained vulnerable to private construction projects. The strategy established stronger local zoning rules, improved mapping, active land acquisition, and revised mitigation policies to protect small-scale urban wetlands.Specific restoration sites targeted in the municipal plan included Pugsley Creek, Soundview Park, Randall’s Island, Calvert Vaux Park, Meadow Lake, Freshkills North Park, and Paerdegat Basin, alongside ongoing ecological stabilization efforts in Jamaica Bay.The framework also encouraged the creation of a natural areas conservancy to coordinate public and private funding for long-term ecological care across the five boroughs.Urban waterways face ongoing ecological pressures from nutrient pollution, particularly high nitrogen levels in treated wastewater discharge. Excessive nitrogen triggers large algal blooms, which deplete dissolved oxygen levels and create dead zones that threaten marine life.At the same time, rising sea levels and intense coastal storms require natural buffer zones to break wave energy and absorb storm surges. Reconstructed tidal marshes, biofiltration swales, and natural stream corridors serve a double purpose by filtering heavy metals and trapping sediment while providing physical flood protection for nearby neighborhoods.By combining Staten Island's natural drainage principles with targeted facility upgrades, local legislation, and biological restoration, the city established a multi-layered urban resilience strategy built to handle changing weather patterns.
Article Summary: In the 1990s, New York chose wetlands over conventional storm sewers on Staten Island. The city’s overarching framework, outlined in the New York City Wetlands Strategy and the PlaNYC 2011 Waterways plan, incorporated natural habitats into the municipal infrastructure toolkit alongside conventional treatment facilities.

Article Title: Trump's hair-do turns heads, has America all tangled up
Article Text:
Donald Trump speaks at an event at the Red Rock Casino Resort and Spa in Las Vegas

TOI correspondent from Washington

mane

: Donald Trump has spent decades insisting that his hair doesn’t just embody style: it is a work of art, a triumph of nature over gravity, and often, an engineering feat involving a comb. This week, however, the 80-year old US President’s famous thinning thatch became theevent of a national discourse.Trump appeared in Las Vegas on Wednesday with a hairstyle that looked noticeably brighter, fuller, and more voluminous than it had the previous day. It achieved new colors and dimensions over the next few days. Whether it was flattering LED lighting (the initial White House explanation), styling, extensions, or a wig, it generated some hair-raising and hair-splitting speculation as Americans briefly set aside arguments over the economy, foreign policy and immigration to ask: Hair today, gone tomorrow?The internet, where facts don’t stand a chance against jokes and memes, decided, “we can’t be LED up a garden path” and blew the bouffant to monstrous proportions. Within hours, social media was awash with AI-generated Trump sporting gigantic 1980s pompadours, wildly exaggerated wigs, tornado-shaped towers, flowing locks, and enough blonde volume to qualify for a wind advisory.Trump’s cabinet members were pulled into the net and given extravagant makeovers with locks and mops, buns and braids, as trolls went on a hairy-fairy excursion. “Make Big Hair Great Again” became an instant slogan.Another meme riffed on Phil Collins: “I can feel it coming in the hair tonight.” And, because no geopolitical crisis is complete without a bad pun, the Strait of Hormuz became the “Strait of Hairmuz,” and worse, “Strait of Hair Mousse. ”The march of follicles was triggered in part because Trump himself has spent years supplying the punchlines. In 2011, he explained that he washes his hair with Head & Shoulders and lets it air-dry, insisting that his trademark style was not really a comb-over but something “a little bit forward and back” – which probably explains his tariff policy and war on Iran. His coiffure was not just hair – it became a glowing symbol of his brand, held together by sheer willpower, industrial-grade lacquer, and a refusal to let any strand part ways with the scalp. He also called his hair a “work of art” and described it as “perfect,” leaving comedians asking: does he ever have a bad hair day?There is something almost historically appropriate about Trump’s ongoing hair loom and doom. Presidents have been mocked for their clothes, voices, ears, eyebrows and facial expressions. But 45-47 has made himself more joke-ready than any president in American history because he has turned his own appearance, personality, and personal mythology into part of his political offensive. His grandiose claims, his demeaning nicknames for rivals, his obsession with television, his love of branding and his extraordinary pride and vanity in his own appearance have made him vulnerable to the oldest rule of comedy: Bigger the self-importance, more lethal the jokes.And perhaps that is the final lesson from the Great Trump Hair Fair of 2026. Presidents may control armies, nuclear arsenals and the global economy. They may command the attention of Congress, Wall Street, and foreign capitals. But no one - not even Donald Trump - can control a nation equipped with AI, Photoshop, social media, and an unlimited supply of hair puns.
Article Summary: Donald Trump has spent decades insisting that his hair doesn’t just embody style: it is a work of art, a triumph of nature over gravity, and often, an engineering feat involving a comb. This week, however, the 80-year old US President’s famous thinning thatch became theevent of a national discourse.

Article Title: In the 1960s, Florida drained land for a giant subdivision; in 2026, restoration finished after removing 260 miles of roads and plugging 48 miles of canals across 55,000 acres
Article Text:
Restoration work at Picayune Strand is helping restore wetlands across 55,000 acres in Southwest Florida.

Restoration changed flow

Long-term benefits

A major restoration project in Southwest Florida has been completed after years of work to bring the natural flow of water back to 55,000 acres of wetlands.According to officials, the Picayune Strand Restoration Project covers area between Alligator Alley and Tamiami Trail in Southwest Florida. It is part of the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan (CERP) which aims at restoring the Everglades ecosystem.The history of the site goes back to the early 1960s, when the land was drained in anticipation of what was intended to become the largest residential subdivision in the world.The drainage changed the natural flow of water across the area. The Picayune Strand project was designed to reverse those changes by removing roads, blocking canals and restoring water movement through the wetlands.The restoration involved major changes to the land and its water network. More than 260 miles of roads were removed, almost 50 miles of canals were plugged and more than 60 miles of logging tram roads were removed. Three pump stations were also constructed as part of the project.The aim was to restore the natural movement of water across the area. The work is expected to improve water flows towards Collier Seminole State Park, the Ten Thousand Islands National Wildlife Refuge and the Rookery Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve.It is also expected to improve wetlands, water quality and habitat for fish and wildlife, including the Florida panther.The Picayune Strand project focused on restoring the natural flow of water across the 55,000-acre area. This was important because the wetlands are part of the wider Everglades ecosystem.The project removed more than 260 miles of roads that had altered the landscape. It also plugged almost 50 miles of canals. More than 60 miles of logging tram roads were removed as well.These changes allow water to move through the area in a way that is closer to its natural flow. The restoration is expected to reduce drainage from nearby sensitive ecosystems and improve the flow of freshwater to downstream areas.The project is also expected to improve aquifer recharge. Aquifers are underground areas that store water. Better recharge can help protect underground water supplies and prevent saltwater from moving into them.The restoration is expected to strengthen wetlands, improve habitat for fish and wildlife, and restore water flows to nearby protected areas, including Collier Seminole State Park, the Ten Thousand Islands National Wildlife Refuge and the Rookery Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve.Florida officials said the project is already improving water quality and wildlife habitat. "Thanks to the support of Governor Ron DeSantis and the Florida Legislature and their steadfast commitment to Everglades restoration, we are seeing what is possible when state and federal governments, along with our partners, commit to this work and follow through," said Alexis A Lambert, Secretary of the Florida Department of Environmental Protection.The restoration is expected to provide several long-term benefits to Southwest Florida. These include restored wetlands, improved habitat for fish and wildlife, reduced drainage of sensitive ecosystems and better aquifer recharge.The project is also expected to reduce freshwater releases and improve the health of downstream estuaries. These benefits are intended to protect the region's natural resources for future generations.The completion of Picayune Strand comes as other Everglades restoration projects have also reached major milestones. Recent work has included the completion of the Biscayne Bay Coastal Wetlands Project. That project is aimed at improving the health of Biscayne Bay, supporting wetland rehydration, improving water quality and building coastal resilience in Miami-Dade County.Officials have also broken ground on the Everglades Agricultural Area Reservoir Inflow Pump Station in Palm Beach County. The station will have the ability to move about 3 billion gallons of water a day from Lake Okeechobee into the EAA Reservoir.Another project, the Blue Shanty Flow Way in Miami-Dade County, is intended to deliver clean water south across Tamiami Trail and into Florida Bay. The Caloosahatchee (C-43) Reservoir in Hendry County has also started operations.A separate agreement between the State of Florida and the US Department of the Army is aimed at speeding up Everglades restoration, including the EAA Reservoir. Under the agreement, the construction timeline for the EAA Reservoir was brought forward by five years, from 2034 to 2029.
Article Summary: The Picayune Strand Restoration Project covers area between Alligator Alley and Tamiami Trail in Southwest Florida. It is part of the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan (CERP) which aims at restoring the Everglade ecosystem. The project removed more than 260 miles of roads that had altered the landscape. It also plugged almost 50 miles of canals and more than 60 miles of logging tram roads.

Article Title: Trump ready to end Iran war without nuclear deal; Tehran's demands complicate exit: Report
Article Text:
Trump is willing to end the Iran war without a nuclear deal but exit strategy remains complicated, report

Domestic pressure mounts

Frozen assets complicate discussions

US President Donald Trump has reportedly signalled to senior aides that he is willing to end the Iran war without securing a nuclear deal with Tehran. But Iran's new demands for reopening the Strait of Hormuz have complicated the US president's efforts to find an exit from the conflict, Wall Street Journal reported Sunday.For weeks, Trump had been preparing to declare victory if Iran fully reopened the strategic waterway, according to US officials cited by the WSJ. The administration had increasingly focused on restoring commercial traffic through the strait after broader negotiations over Iran's nuclear programme proved difficult.But Tehran has now raised the price for reopening the waterway, demanding billions of dollars in US payments, the withdrawal of American forces from the region and an end to the US naval blockade, among other concessions, the report said.Iranian Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr said on Saturday that Tehran would require the US to permanently end the war, lift its naval blockade, withdraw its forces, end sanctions, release Iran's frozen assets and pay war reparations before the strait could be reopened, according to Iranian state news agency IRNA.Iran has also demanded an end to US threats and military action against its regional allies.The developments threaten to narrow Trump's options for securing an exit from the conflict. The president has repeatedly threatened a major escalation of the US bombing campaign while also signalling that he wants the war to end.“The Iranians fully believe Trump wants out and is focused on opening the strait, which is why they are playing hardball,” Gregory Brew, an Iran expert at Eurasia Group, told the WSJ.Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East programme at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said Iran's demands were making it increasingly difficult for Trump to find a politically acceptable way out of the conflict.The Strait of Hormuz has become a central point of leverage for Tehran. Iran closed the waterway after the war began in February, disrupting commercial shipping through a route that is critical to global energy supplies.Trump has repeatedly claimed in recent weeks that the strait was open, but those declarations have come before commercial traffic was fully restored.The issue has taken on added urgency for Trump with US gasoline prices remaining above pre-war levels and the midterm elections less than three months away.Trump has also increasingly suggested that a nuclear agreement may not be necessary for him to declare the conflict successfully concluded.On Friday, he shared a social-media post linking to an article declaring that “Donald Trump Won the Iran War.”Vice President JD Vance similarly indicated that Washington would continue applying pressure on Tehran but said the administration could accept the absence of further negotiations if Iran did not agree to its demands.The White House has said US forces have achieved their military objectives in Iran. A White House official told the WSJ that Trump's focus had now shifted to ensuring the free movement of energy through the Strait of Hormuz, while military options would remain available if Iran attacks additional vessels.A further complication is the question of money. Iran is seeking billions of dollars in war reparations and the unfreezing of assets held overseas. Trump has said the US would not allow American taxpayer money to be sent to Iran, although the WSJ reported that an agreement could require Washington to release at least some frozen Iranian assets, potentially under conditions.There is also disagreement over whether the US should again allow Iran to sell oil on international markets. Washington had previously granted oil-sale waivers as part of an interim ceasefire agreement, but reinstated sanctions after the ceasefire collapsed following Iranian attacks on shipping in the strait.Trump has privately indicated that Iran's nuclear programme may no longer be an immediate obstacle to ending the war, according to US officials cited by the WSJ. He believes the destruction of three major Iranian nuclear sites has severely impaired Tehran's ability to restart its programme and that US intelligence would detect attempts to rebuild them or secretly develop a weapon.If Iran's nuclear capabilities remain contained and commercial traffic through Hormuz resumes, Trump is more likely to extend the current ceasefire indefinitely, the officials said.The administration is also expected to lift its blockade of Iranian ports if Tehran fully reopens the strait.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump is willing to end the Iran war without a nuclear deal, the Wall Street Journal reported. But Iran's new demands for reopening the Strait of Hormuz have complicated the US president's efforts to find an exit from the conflict.

Article Title: Universal Studios is using ‘goats’ to reduce the risk of wildfires that usually comes with the brutal Californian summers
Article Text:
Image Credit: Mjrichmo/Wikipedia

Why the Universal Studios is using a goat crew for fire resistance

Entrance to the theme park. Image Credit: Wikipedia

What does the research say about grazing and fire prevention

Which environment is favorable for these grazing animals to excel at their job

A two-month-old calf in a field of capeweed. Image Credit: Wikipedia

What are the practical limits of using goats

How are these herds managed and protected on the job

Summers in California is officially the annual wildfire season, marked by destruction and the loss of infrastructure. In response to this threat, land managers and organisations are shifting from machines to natural solutions for protecting sensitive landscapes. One popular example is ‘Universal Studios Hollywood,’ which has started using a massive herd of hungry goats to protect its iconic production lot and surrounding hillsides.This approach is known as targeted grazing, and involves using animals to eat a lot of dry brush and overgrown vegetation that would act as fuel for fast-moving flames. By including these goats in the safety protocols, the studio aims to create a more resilient environment. This method represents a shift towards eco-friendly land management that balances modern safety requirements with tradition.‘The Independent’ reports that almost 500 goats have returned to Universal Studios for the second year in a row. Instead of being in a new movie production, these goats are assigned an important role in wildfire prevention across hundreds of acres of hills. This season, the herd successfully cleared 77 acres of dense vegetation in just one month, consuming thousands of pounds of wildfire fuel every day.Jorden Anderson, a senior director at the Studio, explained that using animals is much safer than gas-powered machinery. Equipment like mowers and hand tools, can accidentally flip rocks or produce sparks from exhaust systems, which creates a serious danger in dry conditions. By employing goats, the studio removes the risk of machine fires while managing the brush that can grow as high as six feet.Scientific evidence supports this natural method as a viable way to mitigate risk. Information compiled by ‘Rent A Goat’ indicates that the goats do not stop wildfires entirely, but well-managed grazing can significantly reduce the fuel that allows flames to spread. A 2014 review published in the journal iForest says that targeted grazing is an effective, low-cost, and non-polluting way to manage wildfire fuels.The review found out that goats are expert at consuming flammable material smaller than a quarter of an inch, such as dry grasses and pine needles. Furthermore, goats also help in reducing ‘ladder fuels’ (the low brush and branches that allow ground fires to climb into the tree canopy). This creates a safe gap between the ground and the treetops, making fires easier to manage.Goats have a distinct advantage on terrain that is difficult for humans to navigate. They are particularly effective on steep, rocky slopes and deep canyons where heavy machinery would be unsafe to operate. These animals are also ideal for the ‘wildland-urban interface’(the brushy boundary where residential neighbourhoods meet open spaces).Because goats consume the vegetation on the spot, there is no need for crews to take away heavy loads of cut material, which simplifies the clearing process. They also provide an eco-friendly method for clearing land near waterways where the use of chemical herbicides is restricted. This makes them a versatile solution for landscapes in California.While the benefits are many, experts emphasize that goats are not a ‘one-time cure’ for fire danger. It is important to understand that no service can make a property entirely fireproof, because vegetation can naturally grow back, requiring seasonal repetition of the grazing. Goats are also limited in what they can eat; they do not remove large trees or dead standing timber.Furthermore, some land managers argue that grazing can become impractical or costly when applied to extremely large areas of land. For organisations like Universal Studios, the most successful result comes from using goats as a ‘first pass’ maintenance tool within a future safety plan. This complete strategy usually includes mechanical work, hand crews to trim higher branches, and hardening structures to make them more fire resistant.‘The Independent’ highlights the human element and the management of these large herds, noting that the operation at Universal is run by a family-owned business called Fire Grazers. Managed by Michael Choi and his brothers, the company was passed down from their father and has grown exponentially as demand for natural fire prevention increases.The herd is not just a group of workers, it is a growing community, with 30 baby goats born right on the Universal Studios Lot this year. The company employs two guardian dogs named Noni and Joy, to ensure the safety of the herd from local predators like coyotes. These dogs roam around the hillsides day and night, making sure that the goats graze in peace. Areas which were cleared last year have seen the return of native plants and decline of the invasive weeds, giving birth to a healthier and more manageable landscape.
Article Summary: Universal Studios Hollywood has started using a massive herd of hungry goats to protect its iconic production lot and surrounding hillsides. This approach is known as targeted grazing, and involves using animals to eat a lot of dry brush and overgrown vegetation. This season, the herd successfully cleared 77 acres of dense vegetation in just one month, consuming thousands of pounds of wildfire fuel every day.

Article Title: Ex-US President Joe Biden’s cancer ‘painful, spread into his bones and further’, says son Hunter
Article Text:
Joe Biden's cancer has metastasized into his bones and further, said his son Hunter

Former US President Joe Biden's prostate cancer has spread beyond his bones and is causing significant pain, his son Hunter Biden said in a BBC interview recently.“The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further,” Hunter Biden told BBC's Newsnight, adding “It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects.”Hunter Biden became emotional while discussing his father's health and said the condition had been difficult to watch. "It’s really, really hard, and it’s really sad to watch,” he said.Biden, 83, revealed in May last year, less than four months after leaving the White House, that he had been diagnosed with an “aggressive form” of prostate cancer that had already spread to his bones.He later underwent radiation treatment and hormone therapy. A Biden spokesman said in October that he was receiving the treatments, while Biden had described his treatment as going “really well” last month.Hunter Biden said his father continued to remain active despite the illness. “He’s still out there. He’s still doing his thing... he so believes in this country,” he said.Biden's health had faced scrutiny during his 2021-25 presidency, particularly after his poor performance in a June 2024 debate against Donald Trump.Biden, then 81, withdrew from the 2024 presidential race following pressure from Democrats, and Trump went on to defeat Vice President Kamala Harris, who became the Democratic nominee.Biden served as US president from 2021 to 2025 and was previously vice president under Barack Obama from 2009 to 2017. His presidential memoir is scheduled for release on November 17.Before Hunter Biden’s remarks, former First Lady Jill Biden had also spoken about Joe Biden’s health, saying he was waking up “seven times a night” before his diagnosis. She said she had raised concerns with White House doctors but thought the issue had been addressed. Jill said Biden will “forever live with cancer” and now undergoes testing every three months along with medication.
Article Summary: Former US President Joe Biden's prostate cancer has spread beyond his bones and is causing significant pain, his son Hunter Biden said in a BBC interview. Hunter Biden became emotional while discussing his father's health and said the condition had been difficult to watch. Biden, 83, revealed in May last year that he had been diagnosed with an “aggressive form” of prostate cancer.

Article Title: In 2023, Hoboken opened a 5.4-acre park on a former industrial site; its playgrounds and lawns can hold up to 2 million gallons of stormwater
Article Text:
City of Hoboken opens New Jersey’s largest resiliency park

"I am incredibly thrilled to celebrate the grand opening of ResilienCity Park, a testament to our City's unwavering commitment to both our residents and the environment,"

"This park opening is a significant milestone in our ongoing efforts to create a sustainable and resilient community, serving as the largest resiliency park in our great state and a model for the rest of the county."

How the flood defence works

"We are very pleased be a partner in this grand endeavor which brings parkland to the community and diverts millions of gallons of CSO to our Hoboken Treatment Plant, thus reducing the amount of untreated wastewater going into the river.

The park, the storage tank below it, and the attendant pump station contribute to a cleaner waterway and bring us one, very big step closer to a truly recreational Hudson River."

City of Hoboken opens New Jersey’s largest resiliency park

Financing and broader climate strategy

"Today we are cutting the ribbon on a project that is a shining example of community investment at its best – building the green infrastructure of tomorrow and an innovative stormwater management system that will reduce the risk of devastating floods, while providing Hoboken residents with a new active open space and multi-purpose athletic fields.

I was proud to advocate for $10 million in FEMA funding that helped make this project a reality, in partnership with the city, state, and county, as we work to meet the climate challenges of the 21st century head on.

"

"Not only were we able to contribute to new open space in a corner of the city that desperately needs it, but we are also able to support flood mitigation in Hoboken again with Trust dollars—something our administration has supported since Super Storm Sandy’s devastating impact on Hoboken back in 2012."

"By reclaiming contaminated land to provide recreational opportunities and mitigate flooding, this remarkable park exemplifies the creative ideas communities across New Jersey, with the DEP’s help, are implementing to respond to the impacts of climate change – and it truly embodies the resilient spirit of the people of Hoboken."

"With the unveiling of ResilienCity Park, the City of Hoboken showcases its commitment to sustainable infrastructure and innovative solutions that protect people from hazardous flooding. As a pioneer in the Cities Race to Zero and with its nation-leading Rebuild by Design initiative, Hoboken continues to lead on climate adaptation and serves as an inspiring resilience blueprint for cities everywhere."

Expansion plans across the city

In 2023, Hoboken opened a 5.4-acre park on a former industrial site. Its playgrounds and lawns can hold up to 2 million gallons of stormwater. Located at 12th and Madison Streets, ResilienCity Park is New Jersey’s largest resiliency park. It has turned a once-blighted site into a public space that serves two purposes: providing recreation and helping protect the city from flash flooding caused by extreme weather, according to the City of Hoboken.The park’s flood-control system combines features above ground with underground storage to protect low-lying areas in western Hoboken. In these areas, rain of more than 0.8 inches per hour can usually cause streets and basements to flood. Funding for the project came from federal, state, and county sources, allowing the park to be completed without increasing the municipal tax levy.The site officially opened after a ribbon-cutting ceremony attended by local, state, and federal officials, including Mayor Ravi S. Bhalla, Governor Phil Murphy, and US Senator Bob Menendez.said Mayor Bhalla.During heavy rain, the park absorbs extra water through green infrastructure and sends it into a 1-million-gallon underground detention tank. Another 1 million gallons can be stored above ground through rain gardens, a basketball court designed to act as a detention basin, and a special cistern that stores water for irrigation at the park.After a storm, a 30-million-gallon-per-day flood pump, built in partnership with the North Hudson Sewerage Authority, moves the stored water from the underground tank directly into the Hudson River.Dr. Richard J. Wolff, Executive Director of The North Hudson Sewerage Authority, explained the benefits for local sanitation systems:Along with flood protection, the park includes a multi-purpose athletic field, a playground, open lawn areas, a water spray site, and a terrace pavilion with a cafe and community room.The redevelopment took several years and was paid for through a number of government programs, meaning local taxpayers did not have to cover the cost. Funding included a $10 million grant from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Building Resilient Infrastructure in Communities (BRIC) program, low-interest loans with $2 million in principal forgiveness from the Environmental Protection Agency Clean Water State Revolving Loan Fund through the New Jersey Infrastructure Bank, and $1 million from the Hudson County Open Space Trust Fund.The project is part of the Rebuild by Design initiative, which is funded by the state and the US Department of Housing and Urban Development. Federal officials stressed the importance of targeted investments to help communities adapt to changing climate conditions."I extend my deepest gratitude to the Biden Administration and our congressional delegation for their continued investment in the health and resilience of New Jersey communities, and to the City of Hoboken for its ongoing efforts to expand opportunity among its residents," said Governor Phil Murphy. "The ResilienCity Park – the largest of its kind in the state – will connect New Jerseyans to green, open space while offering our children and families a host of recreational activities. "US Senator Bob Menendez added:US Senator Cory Booker highlighted the wider impact of the project across New Jersey:"ResilienCity Park represents the type of state-of-the-art resilient infrastructure New Jersey needs to mitigate the impact of climate change, such as extreme flooding and sea level rise. I am proud to have secured federal investment for this project and will continue fighting for funding so we can better protect our communities."Hudson County Executive DeGise said the Hudson County Open Space Trust Fund saw the park as providing two major benefits:Environmental leaders also described the site as an example that other communities could follow. Shawn M. LaTourette, Commissioner of Environmental Protection, praised the transformation:Angie Fyfe, Executive Director of ICLEI USA, added:ResilienCity Park is the third resiliency installation in Hoboken since 2017. It follows the Southwest Resiliency Park and the 7th & Jackson Resiliency Park. Together, the first two parks can hold 670,000 gallons of stormwater.City officials plan to double the Southwest Resiliency Park from 1 acre to 2 acres. This would increase its stormwater capacity from 200,000 gallons to 510,000 gallons. Public planning and design are also underway for a fourth park at 800 Monroe Street. Once these projects are finished, Hoboken will have added about 10 acres of resiliency parkland to its urban area since 2016.
Article Summary: City of Hoboken opens New Jersey’s largest resiliency park. The 5.4-acre park is on a former industrial site. Its playgrounds and lawns can hold up to 2 million gallons of stormwater. Funding for the project came from federal, state, and county sources.

Article Title: ICE arrests over 1,200 illegal immigrants in Georgia; sex offenders, child abusers among those held
Article Text:
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)

ICE: Operation targeted criminal offenders

Trucking company among locations targeted

ICE steps up enforcement

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested 1,226 illegal immigrants in Georgia during an enhanced enforcement operation targeting individuals with criminal histories, according to the agency.Dubbed “Operation Safe Community–Atlanta,” the operation resulted in the arrest of 720 people who had either been convicted of or charged with crimes in the US, ICE said.The agency said the arrests involved offences including sex crimes, crimes against children, aggravated assault, drug offences, burglary, weapons violations and driving under the influence.“Our officers did what they do best: They arrested and removed dangerous criminal offenders from American communities,” ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Acting Assistant Director Patricia Hyde said in a statement.ICE said all 1,226 individuals arrested during the operation were in violation of US immigration law, while more than 700 also had criminal histories in the country.ICE officers also arrested five illegal immigrants at the address of a trucking company that the agency said was known for employing illegal immigrants.Among those arrested was Fabian Pineda-Garcia, a Mexican national with prior convictions for conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute at least 500 grams of methamphetamine and driving while intoxicated, according to ICE.The agency also identified Jose Felix Amaya-Pineda, from El Salvador, who had prior arrests for domestic battery/family violence, cruelty to children, disorderly conduct and driving while intoxicated.Other arrests included Elena Marin, a Romanian national with prior arrests for theft by deception and petit larceny, and Armando Loma-Cristo, a Mexican national previously arrested on allegations including DUI, supplying alcohol to underage people, child endangerment and driving without a valid licence, ICE said.The Georgia operation comes as the Trump administration continues to intensify immigration enforcement across the US.ICE has been carrying out targeted operations against illegal immigrants with criminal records, with the agency saying the efforts are aimed at removing dangerous offenders from American communities.
Article Summary: 1,226 illegal immigrants arrested in Georgia during enhanced enforcement operation. Arrests involved offences including sex crimes, crimes against children, aggravated assault, drug offences, burglary, weapons violations and driving under the influence. Operation comes as the Trump administration continues to intensify immigration enforcement across the US.

Article Title: LeT man dies in Pakistan after meal, speculation of poisoning
Article Text:
Qari Saeed Abdul Aziz had played a key role in the planning of many terror strikes, including the 26/11 Mumbai attack

LeT operative was involved in the 26/11 Mumbai attack

A high-ranking Lashkar-e-Taiba operative is learnt to have died under mysterious circumstances, leaving many in Islamabad intrigued.Qari Saeed Abdul Aziz, who was involved in the planning of the 26/11 Mumbai terrorist attacks, collapsed and died near the entrance of a mosque in the Pakistan capital on August 8.Local media reports indicated Abdul Aziz had dined at an unfamiliar location shortly before arriving at the mosque.Within moments of reaching the gate, he suddenly collapsed and was pronounced dead on the spot, with the exact cause of his demise remaining unclear. The local administration has not denied poisoning.Qari Saeed Abdul Aziz, who died mysteriously Sunday, was a pivotal figure within terror outfit Lashkar-e-Taiba, having played a key role in the planning of many terror strikes, including the 26/11 Mumbai attack.Within the organisation, he directed a dedicated division responsible for maintaining active communications and managing financial support for families of terrorists killed during encounters with security forces in J&K. His sudden death has drawn attention from regional intelligence observers. While the timeline between his meal at an unknown location and his subsequent collapse has prompted speculation about potential targeted poisoning, experts note that a severe medical emergency cannot be ruled out.
Article Summary: Qari Saeed Abdul Aziz, who was involved in the planning of the 26/11 Mumbai terrorist attacks, collapsed and died near the entrance of a mosque in the Pakistan capital on August 8. Local media reports indicated he had dined at an unfamiliar location shortly before arriving at the mosque. The exact cause of his demise remains unclear.

Article Title: From 'enemies' to 'patriotic brothers': Pakistan changes stance on PoK protesters ahead of polls
Article Text:
Pakistan PML-N has softened its stance on PoK protesters, calling them "patriotic brothers", as the party prepares to form a government in the region.

Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ’s led PML-N appears to be softening its position towards protesters in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), with a senior government adviser now describing the vast majority of demonstrators as “patriotic” and saying the party will soon engage with them.Sharif’s adviser Rana Sanaullah on Saturday said 99 per cent of those associated with the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), the group leading months of protests in the region, were “our patriotic brothers”.“When the PML(N) government will be formed with two-third majority, it will sit with [Joint Awami] Action Committee representatives. Their first task will be to resolve this issue,” Sanaullah said at a rally ahead of the third and final phase of elections in PoK.The remarks mark a notable shift from the government's earlier rhetoric towards the protesters.Just days earlier, Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif had likened the protesters to India and described them as “enemies of Pakistan”, ruling out talks with them. Asif had said there would be “no dialogue with the protesters” and that he considered them in the same category as India.India, however, has rejected Pakistan's stance on the unrest, saying the protests are a direct consequence of Pakistan's economic exploitation, denial of fundamental rights and administrative oppression in PoK.Sanaullah had also previously accused the protesters of seeking to seize Muzaffarabad and Mirpur by force and described their actions as an “India-like attack”. The government had disputed claims of civilian deaths during clashes and accused protesters of opening fire at security personnel.The JAAC, however, has alleged that security forces opened fire on its activists during protests and long marches, with the group claiming that more than 40 people, including women and children, had been killed since elections began and around 400 protesters had been killed since early June.The Pakistan government has rejected the JAAC's figures as “overly exaggerated”, though Sanaullah has acknowledged that the number of people killed in the protests was in the “two digits” and that security personnel had also died.The change in tone comes as the PML-N prepares to take charge of the so-called government in PoK following elections that have been accompanied by violence and allegations of rigging.In the first two phases of voting, the PML-N has won 25 of the 45 directly elected seats, crossing the majority mark in the so-called legislative assembly. The party is in a direct contest with the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), its coalition partner in Pakistan's federal government.The third and final phase of polling for four seats is scheduled for Monday, while elections in seven constituencies have been indefinitely postponed.The JAAC has been leading protests in PoK since June, drawing support from students, traders, transporters, lawyers and social workers. The regional government banned the group in June.The protests have faced a security crackdown, with Amnesty International and the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan raising concerns over reports of violence and calling for investigations.The situation also drew concern from the United Nations, when it called for accountability for actions against people engaged in peaceful protest.The United States has also urged Pakistan to exercise restraint amid the unrest, calling on authorities to respect fundamental freedoms and create conditions for free and fair elections.
Article Summary: Pakistan PML-N appears to be softening its position towards protesters in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) A senior government adviser has now described the vast majority of demonstrators as “patriotic” The remarks mark a notable shift from the government's earlier rhetoric towards the protesters.

Article Title: 'Shouldn't be exclusive club': Pak minister seeks Nato-like Islamic military alliance
Article Text:
"I put the protesters of PojK in the same category as India and consider them as enemies," Khawaja Asif said.

A day after Pakistan signed a defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif on Saturday called for Islamic countries to set aside their differences and form a military alliance along the lines of Nato.In an interview with Geo News, Asif said the agreement signed in Mecca should not remain an "exclusive club" and should be expanded to include other Islamic countries."See, we can't close the doors for other countries. This shouldn't be an exclusive club. This is my personal opinion. It should expand," Asif said."I think Muslim countries should keep their differences, transactional or bilateral disputes aside, on the lines of Nato and stand together," he added.Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey signed the defence pact in Mecca on Friday, marking a significant strategic development in the region. The agreement reportedly commits the three countries to regard an armed attack against any one of them as an attack against all three, drawing comparisons with Nato's Article 5 collective-defence principle.The pact brings together Saudi Arabia's financial strength, Turkey's defence industry and Nato experience, and Pakistan's large military and nuclear capabilities.According to Pakistan's foreign ministry, the agreement is "guided by the longstanding historical ties among the three states" and their shared strategic interests, defence cooperation and "enduring bonds of brotherhood and Islamic solidarity".The agreement aims to strengthen collective deterrence against aggression and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three countries would be regarded as an attack against all, according to a joint statement.The pact comes as Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries face missile attacks and disruptions to energy shipments amid the ongoing conflict involving Iran and its regional allies. The conflict escalated after the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran on February 28, triggering a wider regional crisis.A Turkish official said the agreement was purely defensive, was not directed at any particular country and remained open to participation by other regional nations. The official added that it would not replace existing bilateral or multilateral security arrangements.
Article Summary: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey signed the defence pact in Mecca on Friday. The agreement reportedly commits the three countries to regard an armed attack against any one of them as an attack against all three. The pact brings together Saudi Arabia's financial strength, Turkey's defence industry and Nato experience, and Pakistan's large military and nuclear capabilities.

Article Title: 'There needs to be accountability': UN warns Pakistan over crackdown on peaceful PoK protesters
Article Text:
Pakistan's widening crackdown in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) draws international attention. (Photo: ANI)

The United Nations has warned Pakistan and called for accountability for any action taken against people participating in peaceful protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK). This came amid continuing unrest and concerns over restrictions on public gatherings and internet access, a spokesperson for UN secretary-general Antonio Guterres said.Asked whether the UN would seek accountability for the reported crackdown on protesters, deputy spokesman for the secretary-general Farhan Haq said authorities must ensure that people are allowed to exercise their right to peaceful protest.“It’s important that all authorities everywhere allow for peaceful protest, and certainly that is the case here. If there have been people harmed for engaging in peaceful protest, there needs to be accountability for that,” Haq told PTI.“The Secretary-General supports the work of his high commissioner, and we certainly hope that the pleas made by Mr Turk will be listened to,” he added.UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Turk had last month expressed concern over the escalating unrest in PoK and called for prompt, thorough and impartial investigations into deaths among both protesters and security personnel.According to the UN, dozens of people, mostly protesters but also members of the law enforcement agencies, had reportedly been killed since June as tensions rose ahead of elections to the legislative assembly.Turk had also called for calm and urged authorities to address the underlying grievances of the local population through meaningful and inclusive political dialogue.The UN human rights chief further criticised Pakistan’s decision to ban the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) and arrest some of its leaders.The JAAC, a coalition of traders, transporters, students, lawyers, activists and other groups, has been leading protests over political and economic issues in the region.The UN also raised concerns over restrictions on internet access and public gatherings, warning that such measures could undermine the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.“We urge the authorities to ensure full Internet access throughout the territory,” the UN statement said.The comments from the UN come amid heightened tensions in PoK, where protests and violence have also disrupted the regional election process.The JAAC has alleged that more than 40 people were killed during the first phase of polling on July 27 and has claimed that around 400 protesters have been killed since the first week of June. The Pakistan government has rejected the figures as “overly exaggerated”.“The number of people killed in the protests is in two digits. Moreover, security personnel have also lost their lives,” Pakistan Prime Minister’s adviser Rana Sanaullah said in a recent television interview.The unrest has also affected the election process in PoK. Authorities on Friday postponed voting indefinitely in seven of the 11 constituencies scheduled to vote in the third phase on August 10, citing concerns over the law-and-order situation. The first two phases of polling, held on July 27 and August 2, were marred by violent protests and allegations of rigging.
Article Summary: The United Nations has warned Pakistan and called for accountability for any action taken against people participating in peaceful protests. This came amid continuing unrest and concerns over restrictions on public gatherings and internet access. UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Turk had last month expressed concern over the escalating unrest in PoK.

Article Title: 'Exercise restraint, act according to law': US urges Pakistan amid PoK crackdown
Article Text:
Representative image

United States on Friday urged the Pakistan government to exercise restraint amid its ongoing crackdown on citizens following violent protests.Speaking to news agency ANI, a US state department spokesperson urged Pakistani authorities to create conditions for free and fair elections that can be conducted peacefully."As with electoral proceedings around the world, we urge officials to create the conditions for free and fair elections that can be conducted in a peaceful manner, including ensuring access to information," the spokesperson said.The state department also called on local authorities to exercise restraint and act in accordance with the country's laws and Constitution."We call on all protesters to express their grievances peacefully, and we call on local authorities to exercise restraint, act in accordance with their country's laws and Constitution, and respect fundamental freedoms as they seek to maintain order," the spokesperson added.The remarks came as at least 30 people, including protesters, security personnel and bystanders, were killed in clashes during June and July.The banned Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) has been staging protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) since June over the contentious 12 refugee seats. It has alleged that Pakistan's establishment manipulates these seats to install a prime minister of its choice to lead the so-called PoK government.According to JAAC, more than 40 people were killed during the first phase of polling on July 27. It also claims that around 400 protesters have been killed since the first week of June.The Shehbaz Sharif government has rejected the claims, calling the figures "overly exaggerated"."The number of people killed in the protests is in two digits. Moreover, security personnel have also lost their lives," Prime Minister's Adviser Rana Sanaullah said in a recent television interview.Meanwhile, voting in seven of the 11 constituencies scheduled for the third phase of polls in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir on August 10 has been postponed indefinitely due to "concerns over the law-and-order situation", authorities announced on Friday.After the first and second phases of polling, which were marred by violent protests, were held on July 27 and August 2, respectively, voting was scheduled for Monday in 11 constituencies of the Poonch Division in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.There are 53 seats in the so-called PoK Legislative Assembly - 45 are directly elected, while eight are reserved for women, technocrats and clerics.The second phase of polling on August 2 was marred by violence and allegations of rigging. One person was killed and several others were injured. The phase also included voting for the 12 refugee seats, which are at the centre of the ongoing controversy.Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) swept the second phase, winning 16 seats, while Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) secured the remaining five.In the first phase on July 27, PML-N won nine of the 13 seats, while PPP won four. With the first two phases combined, PML-N has already secured 24 seats.
Article Summary: U.S. urges Pakistan to create conditions for free and fair elections that can be conducted peacefully. At least 30 people, including protesters, security personnel and bystanders, were killed in clashes during June and July. Banned Joint Awami Action Committee has been staging protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir since June over the contentious 12 refugee seats.

Article Title: Unknown gunmen kill Pakistani policeman, abduct another in separate incidents
Article Text:
The motive behind both the incidents could not immediately be ascertained.

A police constable was shot dead and another was abducted in two separate attacks in Pakistan's northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, officials said on Thursday.The incidents took place late on Wednesday night in Bannu and Tank districts. Police said the motive behind the attacks remains unclear and investigations are under way.In the first incident, Constable Noor Alam, who served in the Special Branch, was killed after unidentified gunmen opened fire on him while he was travelling from his home to report for duty in Bannu district.According to police, Alam regularly used the same route to reach his workplace. He was attacked near Masoomabad on the Bannu-Miranshah Road within the jurisdiction of Cantt Police Station. The assailants fled immediately after carrying out the shooting.In a separate incident, Constable Irfanullah, a wireless operator posted at Shaheed Mureed Akbar Police Station, was abducted from his native village of Sheikh Awtar in Tank district while he was on leave.District Police Officer, Tank, said a search operation had been launched and an investigation into the abduction was underway, adding that efforts were being made to ensure the safe recovery of the abducted constable.
Article Summary: The incidents took place late on Wednesday night in Bannu and Tank districts. Police said the motive behind the attacks remains unclear and investigations are under way. In the first incident, Constable Noor Alam was killed after unidentified gunmen opened fire on him while he was travelling from his home.

Article Title: Pakistan's crackdown in PoK: How Islamabad is tightening information chokehold amid global scrutiny
Article Text:
Pakistan imposes strict restrictions on media (ANI photo)

Pakistan's widening crackdown in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) has drawn international attention, with members of the Kashmiri diaspora, rights groups and global watchdogs raising concerns over restrictions on journalists and media freedom.The measures, introduced by the Shehbaz Sharif government during the so-called assembly elections in the illegally-occupied Valley, have also been criticised by press freedom organisations.According to The New York Times, Pakistan has imposed strict rules requiring journalists working for foreign media outlets to seek government permission before travelling outside Islamabad, Karachi and Lahore.The restrictions come amid increased media coverage of protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, where demonstrators have been demanding greater political autonomy since early June.The NYT reported that the restrictions could severely affect independent reporting from Pakistan."Heavy local journalists say will close off one of the last remaining ways to get independent journalism about the world’s fifth-most-populous country," the report said.Pakistan has also ordered journalists working for foreign media organisations to leave PoK immediately."The requirement that journalists obtain state approval to report from large parts of the country sends a chilling message: that critical reporting is unwelcome," Pakistan’s leading human rights organisation said in a statement.Journalists covering developments in PoK have come under particular pressure. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), two independent Pakistani journalists were detained on August 1 and taken to an undisclosed location.Several others have reportedly been summoned to court under a law that criminalises "false and fake information" over their reporting from the region.The new restrictions have also been criticised internationally. Patricia Gossman, Human Rights Watch’s senior associate Asia director, called them an "alarming step in the country’s narrowing space for press freedom and free expression." Pakistan ranks 153rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders Press Freedom Index.The Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists also urged the Sharif-led government to withdraw the restrictions. "If the government is really interested in showing that it believes in democracy and press freedom, then it should immediately lift this ban," the organisation said.Pakistan's ministry of information, however, said foreign media organisations would continue to operate normally and that the government was working on a new system for issuing travel permits.The restrictions are expected to have the biggest impact on reporting from Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, where the election process is scheduled to conclude on August 10.The region has witnessed months of protests demanding constitutional reforms, while authorities accuse protesters of violence and demonstrators accuse security forces of suppressing peaceful protests.According to local officials and independent estimates cited by the NYT, at least 30 people, including protesters, security personnel and bystanders, were killed in clashes during June and July.Meanwhile, India has also strongly condemned the neighbouring Pakistan's crackdown on PoK. The ministry of external affairs called the local elections as "a complete farce." The MEA also highlighted the situation gripped with violence, blackouts, intimidation, and repression against civilians.The Kashmiri diaspora abroad has also staged a strong demonstration in UK. The agitated people took to the streets of Bradford, condemning Pakistan's crackdown in PoK.
Article Summary: Pakistan imposes strict restrictions on media. Restrictions come amid increased media coverage of protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. Kashmiri diaspora abroad has staged a strong demonstration in UK. India has also strongly condemned the neighbouring Pakistan's crackdown on PoK.

Article Title: Imran Khan's three years in jail spark protests across Pakistan; over 100 held
Article Text:
More than 100 supporters of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan have been arrested as rallies were held across Pakistan on Wednesday to mark the completion of three years of his imprisonment.

Peshawar rally sets September 27 deadline

Family, PTI leaders raise detention concerns

Over 100 supporters of jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan were arrested on Wednesday as Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters held rallies nationwide to mark three years of his imprisonment. The demonstrations, which called for Khan’s release, saw police fire tear gas at protesters in Rawalpindi amid clashes and heightened security.The main rally was held in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where PTI is in power. The party demanded Khan’s release and restoration of his rights. Thousands of supporters gathered amid heavy security, according to Al Jazeera.In Punjab, Police baton-charged protesters and arresting scores of PTI workers in Lahore, Mianwali and Rawalpindi. In Lahore's Mall Road, police dispersed demonstrators demanding Khan's release and detained several protesters.Video footage circulated on social media showed rapid response force (RRF) using force against demonstrators. Some journalists covering the rally were also allegedly thrashed by police, prompting protests from media bodies.PTI Punjab general secretary Chaudhry Bilal Ejaz said five party lawmakers were among 25 others arrested in Lahore.“Despite this era of oppression, repression, and fascism, a large number of PTI workers and office-bearers in Punjab staged protest rallies and pledged to stand with Imran Khan,” he told news agency PTI.According to PTI, at least 50 workers were arrested in Mianwali, Rawalpindi and other parts of Punjab. In Karachi, police used tear gas to disperse PTI supporters protesting in Saddar Town and arrested more than 10 demonstrators. The party also claimed six workers were arrested in Pano Aqil and 15 in Kandhkot.On Wednesday, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister Muhammad Suhail Afridi announced that PTI supporters will march towards Islamabad on September 27 if 'justice' is not provided to Khan.Addressing supporters in Peshawar, Afridi said the party's first demand was for cases against Khan and his wife to be heard and decided on merit. Its second demand, he said, was restoration of meetings with their legal team, doctors, relatives and party leaders.He claimed that if justice is delivered, Khan can be released “within 30 minutes”. Otherwise, he said, people from across Pakistan will march to Islamabad on September 27.Aleema Khan, sister of the ousted PM, said the movement for his release had already begun and its next phase would be announced soon.PTI senior leader Moonis Elahi alleged that Khan “has been denied meetings and proper medical treatment, and his eyesight has also deteriorated” in prison.Khan, 73, was arrested on August 5, 2023, and has remained in prison while facing multiple cases. His party has repeatedly alleged that the cases are politically motivated, a charge denied by the Shehbaz Sharif-led government.Amnesty International, a global non-governmental organization, also called on Pakistani authorities to uphold Khan's rights. Acting Regional Director for South Asia Isabelle Lassee said, “For three years, Pakistan’s authorities have systematically denied Imran Khan the right to a fair trial, subjected him to prolonged solitary confinement, and limited his access to medical care and visitation rights.”Lassee further said Khan had not been allowed to meet his family for more than eight months and that he and his wife, Bushra Bibi, had been denied regular access to legal counsel since December 2025.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters held rallies nationwide to mark three years of Imran Khan's imprisonment. The demonstrations, which called for Khan’s release, saw police fire tear gas at protesters in Rawalpindi amid clashes and heightened security. The main rally was held in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Article Title: Peace talks abroad, protests at home: The many contradictions shaping Pakistan today
Article Text:
Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and army chief Asim Munir (R) (PTI file photo)

From military confrontation to diplomatic outreach

The Iran gamble

A war next door, and Pakistan's opportunity

Living on lifelines, dreaming of leadership

Source: IMF

Security ambitions amid diplomatic outreach

Diplomacy abroad, discontent within

Operation Sindoor 's lasting fallout

Operation Sindoor fallout

Sites targeted during Op Sindoor

The Balochistan challenge refuses to fade

BLA

Pakistan's uneasy neighbourhood

Presence of TTP remains a major challenge for Pakistan

A nation seeking influence while confronting instability

"A house divided against itself cannot stand." Abraham Lincoln's observation aptly captures Pakistan 's situation.While Islamabad chases the image of an indispensable diplomatic player, its own foundations appear increasingly fragile. From brokering peace in Middle East to courting Washington and Beijing, Pakistan has sought a larger role in global diplomacy.Yet back home, it remains weighed down by economic distress, political unrest, separatist movements, water shortages, terrorism, and accusations of human rights abuses, an uneasy contradiction that defines the country's present-day reality.Much of Pakistan's strategic direction continues to be shaped by its military establishment, with army chief Asim Munir, the country's de facto centre of power. His influence extends well beyond defence matters, as Pakistan's military continues to function as a parallel authority that heavily influences domestic governance as well as foreign policy.That contrast between projecting stability abroad and confronting instability at home, has become one of Pakistan's defining geopolitical challenges.Just over a year ago, Pakistan suffered one of its most difficult periods on the diplomatic and military fronts following India's response to the Pakistan-backed terror attack in South Kashmir's Pahalgam.New Delhi's "zero-tolerance" policy under Prime Minister Narendra Modi translated into a series of retaliatory actions that once again placed Pakistan under international scrutiny over terrorism.Yet, even as tensions with India remained elevated, Islamabad quickly sought to recast its international image.Already maintaining close ties with China, Pakistan simultaneously attempted to deepen engagement with Donald Trump's United States. For a country grappling with a fragile economy, maintaining goodwill with both Washington and Beijing has become increasingly important.It was in this backdrop that Pakistan pitched itself as a potential mediator between Iran and the United States.Pakistan's bid to position itself as a regional peace broker did not begin smoothly.Its initial attempt to host talks between Iran and the United States faltered after Tehran rejected Islamabad as the venue. According to The Wall Street Journal, Iran formally informed mediators that it would not attend the proposed talks with American officials in Pakistan.Islamabad, however, persisted.Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and military head Asim Munir stepped up engagement with Washington, with Munir's growing proximity to the Trump administration earning him the title of Trump's "favourite field marshal".Around the same time, Sharif attended President Xi Jinping 's grand military parade in Beijing alongside leaders including Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.The event reinforced Pakistan's continued strategic closeness with China even as it simultaneously sought stronger engagement with Washington.Six months later, the geopolitical landscape shifted dramatically as President Donald Trump launched military strikes against Iran, joined by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu under Operation Epic Fury.Global Shia icon and longest-ruling Supreme Leader of Iran Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed on the opening day of the offensive on February 28, 2026 in Pakistan's neighbourhood.The raging Tehran regime's response left the Middle East region totally disturbed. Bombs, missiles and drones fell, almost hitting every country in the region.Retaliatory strikes and military activity engulfed large parts of the region, with airspace disrupted across Iraq, Kuwait, Syria, Lebanon, Yemen, Oman, Jordan, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.However, Pakistan, despite its border with Iran, remained untouched and safe.That made Islamabad a potential venue for talks with Iran's new leadership under Mojtaba Khamenei .Sensing an opportunity, Pakistan declared itself a peace broker. On April 8, Sharif posted on X announcing a ceasefire that actually wasn't close to peace.He wrote: "With the greatest humility, I am pleased to announce that the Islamic Republic of Iran and the United States of America, along with their allies, have agreed to an immediate ceasefire everywhere including Lebanon and elsewhere, EFFECTIVE IMMEDIATELY."In May, army chief Asim Munir hailed the development as "slight progress". US Vice President JD Vance visited Pakistan twice for peace talks, but despite the diplomatic efforts, the fighting continued and a lasting peace remained elusive.Still, the symbolism was already disheartening. The same country where the US carried out Operation Neptune Spear to eliminate Osama bin Laden had now become Washington's chosen venue for talks with Iran.Islamabad may be eager to wear the badge of a global player, but its economic reality tells a far less flattering story. Beneath the grand diplomatic posturing lies a cash-strapped nation surviving on lifelines from China, the United States, the IMF and other international lenders, hardly the profile of a country calling the shots on the world stage.According to Reuters, the IMF in May completed reviews of its lending programmes with Pakistan, clearing the way for approximately $1.32 billion in fresh funding.The package included nearly $1.1 billion under the Extended Fund Facility and around $220 million under the Resilience and Sustainability Facility, taking total disbursements under the two ongoing programmes to roughly $4.8 billion.Pakistan remains under a $7-billion IMF programme after reaching a staff-level agreement in March."Amid a more challenging and highly uncertain external environment since the onset of the war in the Middle East, Pakistan needs to maintain strong macroeconomic policies while accelerating reform efforts," the IMF said in a statement.For Islamabad, therefore, diplomacy is not merely about regional influence. It is also about preserving the confidence of the international community at a time when its economy remains deeply dependent on external financing.Alongside its mediation efforts, Pakistan has also sought to deepen strategic partnerships within the Islamic world.Islamabad has moved closer to Turkey and Saudi Arabia, readying a Nato-style Islamic security arrangement with mutual defence provisions reminiscent to Nato.The defence pact, signed by Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in September, states that "any aggression" against one member would be treated as an attack on all , a provision that closely mirrors Nato's Article 5. Turkey, already a Nato member, fields the alliance's second-largest military after the United States.While the arrangement remains far from becoming a formal military alliance, it reflects Islamabad's broader effort to strengthen its regional security architecture to counter New Delhi.However, the economic and military size of the two-nuclear armed nations still remain widely different.Pakistan lagging far behind.Even with Islamabad's projected flamboyancy in foreign dealings, unrest continues across Pakistan and regions illegally occupied by Pakistan.The most visible flashpoint in recent months has been Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), where the so-called Assembly elections have been conducted in three phases amid allegations of police excesses and restrictions on dissent.Videos and reports emerging from the region have shown violent confrontations between security forces and protesters, prompting criticism from rights groups and attracting international attention.Pakistan's own defence minister, Khawaja Asif, further fuelled controversy with remarks defending the government's actions."I put the protesters of PoJK in the same category as India and consider them as enemies," Asif said.The statement reflected Islamabad's increasingly uncompromising approach towards dissent in the region.The ministry of external affairs strongly denounced Pakistan's mischievous handling of the situation, describing the elections in PoK as a "complete farce". The MEA also condemned the Islamabad-backed ill-treatment and crackdown that killed 90 people in the region since June this year.Human rights organisations have echoed similar concerns.Amnesty International USA called reports emerging from PoK's Rawalakot as "disturbing" and urged Pakistani authorities to restore communication services and permit independent media and observers into the region."The disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot are consistent with the Pakistani authorities' long history of unlawful violence against protesters in PoJK. We urge the Pakistani authorities to restore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area," Amnesty International USA posted on X.The developments have reinforced criticism that, while Islamabad attempts to mediate conflicts abroad, it continues to face accusations of suppressing dissent within territories under its own control.Behind the fancy overcoat of its foreign policy ambitions, Pakistan ultimately bore the brunt of its fertile terror fields it had long nurtured.The fallout from Operation Sindoor did not just damage Pakistan-backed terror camps and military infrastructure.India swiftly showcased the scale of its response, striking nine terror bases and 11 military installations across Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK).The consequences of Operation Sindoor extended beyond military targets to the country's most basic necessities, including water. With all major rivers in Pakistan flowing into its territory from India, New Delhi had placed the decades-old Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance immediately after the Pahalgam massacre of April 22, 2025.The country is facing an increasingly severe water crisis, particularly across Sindh and Balochistan , where shrinking river flows and uneven distribution have triggered alarm among farmers, political leaders and water experts.Months after New Delhi's decision, Pakistan is confronting growing concerns over agricultural losses, declining livelihoods and mounting economic pressure across several provinces.Sindh, home to Karachi, Pakistan's financial capital, has emerged as one of the worst-hit regions, with water shortages threatening agriculture and affecting millions of people.Prime Minister Narendra Modi had encapsulated India's position soon after the Pahalgam attack."Terror and talks cannot go together; water and blood cannot flow together," he had said.The message was reiterated recently by defence minister Rajnath Singh recently on Kargil Vijay Diwas."After the Pahalgam terror attack, by suspending the Indus Waters Treaty, we said that those whose tears have dried up should not expect water from us. We will not let the waters of the Sindhu reach the patrons of terrorists and enemies of humanity," Rajnath said.For Pakistan, the water crisis has added yet another layer to an already fragile economic and political situation, with experts warning that prolonged shortages could further aggravate regional discontent.While PoK has dominated headlines in recent weeks, Balochistan continues to represent Pakistan's longest-running internal security challenge.The province recently announced plans to observe its own Independence Day, underlining the persistence of separatist sentiment.The conflict, rooted in grievances dating back to Balochistan's accession to Pakistan in 1948, revolves around demands for greater political autonomy, control over natural resources and opposition to mega infrastructure projects such as the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC).Over the decades, the conflict has been marked by armed insurgency, heavy militarisation and repeated allegations of human rights violations.Yet Balochistan is only one strand of Pakistan's broader internal unrest.The country's dissent is neither unified nor driven by a single cause.Separatist groups in Balochistan, the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, political activists and unemployed youth often pursue vastly different objectives.That fragmentation, however, has also worked to the advantage of Pakistan's establishment.Without a unified opposition, the state has been able to confront each movement differently, labelling one as terrorism, another as separatism, others as political disorder or foreign conspiracy.Rather than confronting a single nationwide challenge, Islamabad faces multiple disconnected crises, each requiring a different response.For neighbouring Iran, Pakistan has recently struck the chord of "peace", offering itself as a mediator, though the negotiations have yielded almost no progress.Its ties with Tehran, however, have rarely been straightforward. Relations with India remain frozen, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi making New Delhi's position unequivocal: "If there will be talks between India and Pakistan, it will only be on terrorism and PoK."To the west, Pakistan's troubles are no less daunting. Crossborder tensions with Taliban-ruled Afghanistan have intensified, even as Islamabad grapples with a surge in terror attacks at home.Beyond the long-running insurgency in Balochistan, Pakistan faces an increasingly potent threat from the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). While the Afghan Taliban returned to power in 2021, Islamabad's hopes of gaining strategic leverage quickly unraveled. Kabul has refused to dismantle TTP sanctuaries, allowing the outfit to regroup and intensify attacks across Pakistan.The fallout has been severe. Cross-border clashes have become more frequent, while the TTP, an umbrella militant group formed in 2007, continues to challenge the Pakistani state's authority, specifying the irony of a country seeking to broker peace abroad while battling an escalating insurgency at home.Pakistan today finds itself pursuing two parallel realities.On one hand, it is attempting to establish itself as a regional diplomatic player, offering to mediate conflicts, expanding defence partnerships and seeking greater geopolitical relevance.On the other, it continues to wrestle with economic fragility, dependence on IMF assistance, unrest in PoK and Balochistan, a worsening water crisis and an increasingly complex internal security landscape.Adding to these challenges is the country's continued struggle with terrorism.
